question: A bike-sharing company is developing a multi-tier architecture to track the locations of its bicycles during peak hours. The company wants to use these data points in its current analytics platform. A solutions architect must determine the optimal solution to support this architecture. The data points must be accessible through a REST API. Which action fulfills these requirements for storing and retrieving the location data?

options.text: Use Amazon Athena with Amazon S3.
Use Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda.
Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon Redshift.
Use Amazon API Gateway with Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics.

explanations.A: Athena with S3 is wrong because it focuses on the analytics/reporting side, not real-time ingestion. Athena and S3 are great for storing and querying big datasets after the fact, but this pairing does nothing to address how raw, real-time location data actually reaches the system through the required REST API.
explanations.B: API Gateway with Lambda correctly uses API Gateway to expose the REST API and Lambda to process incoming data, but it isn't optimal for a high-volume streaming workload like continuous bike-location updates. A dedicated streaming service is more scalable and less costly than invoking a Lambda function per individual data point.
explanations.C: QuickSight with Redshift is wrong for the same reason as Athena with S3: it's a visualization/analytics pairing, not an ingestion pairing. It doesn't address how the real-time location data gets into the system via the REST API in the first place.
explanations.D: API Gateway with Kinesis Data Analytics is correct because it matches each part of the workload to the most suitable tool. API Gateway provides a scalable REST API endpoint that the bikes send data to. From there, the data is ingested into a Kinesis Data Stream via Kinesis Data Analytics, which is purpose-built for high-volume, real-time streaming. Kinesis Data Analytics can process and analyze the data immediately, before it is stored in S3 or Redshift for the existing analytics platform.

summary: This is about designing a real-time data ingestion and processing pipeline — the crux is finding the optimal mix of services that can handle a large volume of streaming data ingested via a REST API and prepare it for the analytics platform. It's not just about storage; it's about the full flow from entry point to analytics.

question: A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to reduce a company's storage costs. All the company's data is currently in the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. The company must keep all data for at least 25 years. Data from the last 2 years must be highly available and instantly retrievable. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to move objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately.
Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to move objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering; enable the archive option to ensure data is archived into S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to move objects to S3 One Zone-IA immediately, then to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.

explanations.A: Moving data to Glacier Deep Archive immediately is wrong because the company requires the last 2 years of data to be highly available and instantly retrievable. Glacier Deep Archive is designed for long-term archiving with a retrieval time of up to 12 hours, which directly violates that requirement.
explanations.B: This is the correct and recommended solution. It meets all requirements exactly: data stays in S3 Standard for the first 2 years, giving high availability and instant retrieval. After those 2 years, there's no longer a need for instant access, so it can move to the more cost-effective long-term archive class, Glacier Deep Archive. This transition happens automatically via the S3 Lifecycle policy.
explanations.C: Using S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the archive option is wrong. Although Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves data between the standard and infrequent-access tiers, it does NOT automatically move data into Glacier Deep Archive — you must explicitly configure the archive option. More importantly, Intelligent-Tiering's primary purpose is data with changing or unpredictable access patterns, whereas this scenario has a predictable, time-bound transition that's better handled by a standard S3 Lifecycle policy.
explanations.D: Moving to S3 One Zone-IA immediately, then Glacier after 2 years, is wrong. It moves data to S3 One Zone-IA immediately, a low-cost class, but the requirement is that the last 2 years must be highly available. One Zone-IA stores data in only a single Availability Zone and is not considered highly available. It's also not the most cost-effective choice for data that's accessed frequently during those first 2 years.

summary: This is about optimizing storage costs for a long-term data retention policy using S3. The solution lies in matching data-retrieval needs to the appropriate storage class over time, which typically requires S3 Lifecycle policies.

question: A company operates a food delivery service. Because of recent growth, the company's order processing system is experiencing scaling problems during peak traffic hours. The current architecture includes Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that collect orders from an application. A second group of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group fulfills the orders. The order collection process occurs quickly, but the order fulfillment process can take longer. Data must not be lost because of a scaling event. A solutions architect must ensure that the order collection process and the order fulfillment process can both scale adequately during peak traffic hours. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure each Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity to meet its peak workload value.

Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the CPUUtilization metric for each instance in both Auto Scaling groups. Configure a CloudWatch alarm to invoke an Amazon SNS topic to create additional Auto Scaling groups on demand.

Provision two Amazon SQS queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection and the second for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on notifications that the queues send.

Provision two Amazon SQS queues. Use one SQS queue for order collection and the second for order fulfillment. Configure the EC2 instances to poll their respective queues. Scale the Auto Scaling groups based on the number of messages in each queue.

explanations.A: Setting the minimum capacity to the peak workload value is wrong. This causes significant over-provisioning and high cost during off-peak hours. While it guarantees capacity for peak times, it isn't cost-effective or truly scalable.
explanations.B: Using an SNS topic to create additional Auto Scaling groups on demand is wrong. This is an overly complex and inefficient approach. Auto Scaling groups are designed to scale their own capacity automatically based on metrics and policies — there's no need to spin up entirely new groups on demand.
explanations.C: Using two SQS queues but scaling based on "notifications" from the queues is wrong. While using Amazon SQS is the right approach for decoupling the two processes, scaling based on notifications from the queues is vague and isn't the standard scaling trigger — SQS doesn't push notifications for scaling purposes in this way.
explanations.D: This is the correct solution: two SQS queues, scaling the Auto Scaling groups based on the number of messages in each queue. Scaling the EC2 fleet based on SQS queue depth (the ApproximateNumberOfMessages metric) is the standard, well-established pattern: it directly reflects how much work is backed up and waiting. Two separate SQS queues let the fast collection process and the slower fulfillment process scale completely independently of each other, and because SQS durably stores messages until they're processed, no data is lost during a scaling event.

summary: This is about solving a scaling problem for a multi-stage application facing sudden, unpredictable traffic spikes. The solution lies in decoupling the fast order-collection process from the potentially slow order-fulfillment process, so each can scale independently without losing data.

question: A company produces batch data from various databases. The company also produces live streaming data from network sensors and application APIs. The company needs to consolidate all of that data in one place for business analytics. The company needs to process the incoming data and then store it in different Amazon S3 buckets. Teams will later run one-time queries and import the data into a business intelligence tool to display KPIs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Athena for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for the KPIs.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for one-time queries. Use Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for the KPIs.
Use AWS Lake Formation blueprints to define which data can be ingested into the data lake. Use AWS Glue to crawl the source, extract the data, and load it into Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format.
Create custom AWS Lambda functions to move individual records from the databases to an Amazon Redshift cluster.

explanations.A: This is correct: use Amazon Athena for one-time SQL queries and Amazon QuickSight to build dashboards for the KPIs. This is the querying and visualization half of the full solution — it's what lets teams run ad-hoc queries and display business metrics once the data has been staged in S3.
explanations.B: Using Kinesis Data Analytics for "one-time queries" is a mismatch. That service is built for real-time streaming analysis, not ad-hoc SQL querying of already-staged data, so it doesn't fit this part of the requirement.
explanations.C: This is correct: use AWS Lake Formation blueprints to define what data can be ingested into the data lake, and use AWS Glue to crawl the source, extract the data, and load it into S3 in Apache Parquet format. This is the ingestion and preparation half of the full solution — it consolidates both the batch database data and the streaming data into the data lake with minimal custom development.
explanations.D: Creating custom AWS Lambda functions to move individual records from the databases to a Redshift cluster requires heavy custom development to build and maintain, which results in high operational overhead compared to using managed ingestion tools like Lake Formation and Glue.

summary: This question is about designing a cost-effective, low-overhead pipeline that ingests both batch and streaming data into a data lake and supports ad-hoc querying and BI dashboards over it — matching AWS's purpose-built ingestion/prep tools (Lake Formation plus Glue) with its purpose-built querying/visualization tools (Athena plus QuickSight).

question: A company performs monthly maintenance on its AWS infrastructure. During these maintenance activities, the company needs to rotate the credentials for its Amazon RDS for MySQL databases across multiple AWS Regions. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Store the credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use Secrets Manager multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Secrets Manager to rotate the secrets on a schedule.

Store the credentials as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use multi-Region secret replication for the required Regions. Configure Systems Manager to rotate the secrets periodically.
Store the credentials in an Amazon S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE) enabled. Use Amazon EventBridge and Amazon CloudWatch events to invoke an AWS Lambda function to update the credentials.

Encrypt the credentials as secrets by using AWS KMS with multi-Region customer-managed keys. Store the secrets in an Amazon DynamoDB global table. Use an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the secrets from DynamoDB and use the RDS API to update the credentials.

explanations.A: This is the correct and recommended solution. AWS Secrets Manager is specifically designed to store, manage, and automatically rotate secrets, including database credentials. It natively integrates with Amazon RDS for MySQL, enabling automatic rotation out of the box. It also supports multi-Region secret replication, which directly meets the requirement to manage credentials across multiple AWS Regions — all fully managed by AWS, minimizing operational overhead.
explanations.B: Using Parameter Store with rotation is wrong. Although Systems Manager Parameter Store can store SecureStrings, it has no built-in feature to automatically rotate credentials — you'd need custom automation, increasing operational cost. Additionally, "multi-Region secret replication" is a Secrets Manager feature, not a Parameter Store feature.
explanations.C: Storing credentials in S3 with EventBridge and Lambda is wrong. Using an S3 bucket, an EventBridge rule, and a Lambda function to rotate credentials is a manual, custom-built solution. It requires writing and maintaining a Lambda function plus orchestrating the whole pipeline, resulting in significant operational overhead and more room for error.
explanations.D: The KMS plus DynamoDB plus Lambda plus RDS API approach is wrong. This is an extremely manual and complex approach involving multiple services just to build a custom credential-management and rotation solution. It would be very difficult to set up and maintain, and it would have the highest operational overhead of all the options.

summary: This is about securely managing and automatically rotating database credentials across multiple AWS Regions with the least effort possible. Core requirements: security, multi-Region support, and low operational cost.

question: A company hosts an application in a private subnet. The company has already integrated the application with an Amazon Cognito user pool to verify user identities. The company needs to modify the application so that it can securely store user documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Which combination of steps will integrate S3 with the application securely?

options.text: Create a Cognito identity pool to generate secure access tokens/credentials to Amazon S3 for users when they successfully sign in.
Use the existing Cognito user pool alone to generate S3 access tokens for users when they successfully sign in.
Create an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint in the same VPC that hosts the application.
Create a NAT gateway in the VPC that hosts the application. Set an S3 bucket policy to deny any request that did not originate from Amazon Cognito.

explanations.A: This is correct: create a Cognito identity pool to generate temporary AWS credentials for signed-in users. The user pool alone only authenticates identity — it doesn't grant AWS access — so the identity pool is needed on top of it to actually authorize access to S3.
explanations.B: Using the user pool alone to generate S3 tokens misunderstands what user pools do. A Cognito user pool handles authentication only; it isn't designed to issue AWS access credentials, so it can't grant access to S3 on its own.
explanations.C: This is correct: create an S3 VPC endpoint in the same VPC that hosts the application. Since the app is in a private subnet with no internet access, an S3 VPC endpoint lets it reach S3 privately, without needing an internet gateway or NAT device.
explanations.D: Creating a NAT gateway plus a bucket policy that denies requests "not from Cognito" doesn't work. S3 bucket policies can't verify that a request came from Cognito specifically, so this restriction can't actually be enforced this way. A NAT gateway also isn't needed once a VPC endpoint is in place, since the traffic should stay private rather than route out to the internet.

summary: This question is about securely connecting a private-subnet application — already using Cognito for user authentication — to Amazon S3, requiring both temporary AWS credentials for authorized access and a private network path to reach S3 without traversing the internet.

question: A company has a website that sells car parts. The company stores its listings in a database on Amazon RDS. When a part sells, the listing must be removed from the website and a notification must be sent to a group of target systems. Which design should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function triggered when the RDS database is updated to send the information to one Amazon SQS queue, which is consumed by the target systems.
Create an AWS Lambda function triggered when the RDS database is updated to send the information to one Amazon SQS FIFO queue, which is consumed by the target systems.
Subscribe to an RDS event notification and send an Amazon SQS queue that fans out to multiple Amazon SNS topics. Use AWS Lambda functions to update the target systems.
Subscribe to an RDS event notification and send an Amazon SNS topic that fans out to multiple Amazon SQS queues. Use AWS Lambda functions to update the target systems.

explanations.A: Lambda triggered on RDS update with a single SQS queue is wrong. There is no native RDS feature to directly trigger a Lambda function on a database update (this would require a custom solution with database triggers and a proxy, adding complexity). Additionally, a single SQS queue is typically consumed by one or more workers and isn't usually designed for a fan-out pattern to multiple independent target systems.
explanations.B: This has the same core flaw as the plain SQS version: there's no native RDS-to-Lambda trigger. Additionally, using an SQS FIFO queue here is unnecessary — the scenario doesn't require strict message ordering, and FIFO queues have lower throughput and higher cost than standard SQS queues.
explanations.C: RDS event notification fanning out from an SQS queue to multiple SNS topics is architecturally incorrect. The fan-out pattern in AWS messaging services goes from one-to-many starting at SNS: the correct pattern is publishing from one SNS topic to multiple SQS queues, not the reverse. So this design is invalid.
explanations.D: This is the correct design pattern: an RDS event notification to an SNS topic, fanning out to multiple SQS queues, with Lambda functions updating each target. RDS can be configured to send event notifications (like a table change) to an SNS topic. SNS is a publish/subscribe service that lets you fan out a single message to multiple subscribers — in this case, the different target systems. By using separate SQS queues for each target system, you decouple the targets and ensure each processes the message at its own pace. Lambda functions then poll their respective SQS queues and process the data to update the target systems.

summary: This is about creating an event-driven architecture to notify multiple systems when a database record is updated. The goal is to ensure the data reliably reaches several destinations.

question: A company has a small Python application that processes JSON documents and outputs the results to a local SQL database. The application runs thousands of times per day. The company wants to migrate the application to AWS Cloud. The company needs a highly available solution that maximizes scalability and minimizes operational overhead. Which of the following solutions meets these requirements?

options.text: Place the JSON documents into an Amazon S3 bucket. Run the Python code on several Amazon EC2 instances to process the documents. Store the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.

Place the JSON documents into an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an AWS Lambda function to run the Python code and process the documents as soon as they arrive in the S3 bucket. Store the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster.

Place the JSON documents into an Amazon EBS volume. Use EBS Multi-Attach to attach the volume to several Amazon EC2 instances. Run the Python code on the EC2 instances to process the documents. Store the results in an Amazon RDS DB instance.

Place the JSON documents into an Amazon SQS queue. Deploy the Python code as a container on an Amazon ECS cluster configured with the EC2 launch type. Use the container to process SQS messages. Store the results in an Amazon RDS DB instance.

explanations.A: Processing on EC2 instances is wrong. This requires you to manage the underlying servers, including updates, security, and scaling. This raises operational overhead and doesn't provide the scalability and cost-efficiency needed for an app that runs thousands of times daily but may otherwise sit idle.
explanations.B: This is the correct and best-fit solution. Placing JSON documents in S3 is the standard practice for cloud object storage. The key is using AWS Lambda — a serverless compute service — which can be automatically triggered whenever a new object is created in the S3 bucket, running the code without you having to provision or manage any servers. This provides maximum scalability, since Lambda scales automatically to handle thousands of daily invocations, and high availability, since Lambda is inherently multi-AZ. Storing the results in an Amazon Aurora DB cluster provides a highly available, scalable, and fully managed database.
explanations.C: Using EBS Multi-Attach for the JSON files has several problems. EBS volumes aren't ideal for storing many small individual files like JSON documents, and EBS Multi-Attach is primarily meant for block-level storage on a single volume shared by a small number of instances. This solution also still uses EC2, raising operational overhead.
explanations.D: Using SQS plus containers on ECS with the EC2 launch type still requires managing the EC2 instances underneath the ECS cluster, which keeps operational overhead higher than a fully serverless approach.

summary: This is about migrating an application to AWS that runs a high volume of short, recurring tasks. The core requirements are high availability, maximum scalability, and minimal operational overhead.

question: A company has an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job that runs every day at the same time to process data files. The job processes XML data that is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. New data is added to the S3 bucket every day. A solutions architect notices that AWS Glue is processing all the data during each run. What should the solutions architect do to prevent AWS Glue from reprocessing old data?

options.text: Edit the job to use job bookmarks.
Edit the job to delete data after it is processed.
Edit the job by setting the NumberOfWorkers field to 1.
Use the FindMatches ML transform.

explanations.A: Using job bookmarks is correct. AWS Glue job bookmarks track the state of previously processed data across job runs. When the job runs again, AWS Glue uses the bookmark to determine which data has already been processed, and processes only the new data.
explanations.B: Deleting data after processing is a very bad idea. Deleting source data after processing is destructive and prevents any future auditing, historical analysis, or reprocessing if an error occurs.
explanations.C: Setting NumberOfWorkers to 1 will not prevent the job from reprocessing old data. That parameter controls parallelism and performance, not what data is processed.
explanations.D: Using the FindMatches ML transform is used for finding duplicate or matching records within a dataset — a completely different use case from tracking which files have already been processed.

summary: This is about optimizing an AWS Glue ETL job to process only new data and avoid reprocessing old data — a common requirement for incremental data loading. The solution lies in finding the right feature that tracks state and processes only new data.

question: A company has created an image-analysis application in which users can upload photos and add pictures to their images. The application allows users to upload the photos and metadata to identify the images that they want to add. The application uses a single Amazon EC2 instance and Amazon DynamoDB to store the metadata. The application's usage is increasing, and the number of users is growing. The company expects the number of concurrent users to vary significantly depending on the time of day and the day of the week. The company must ensure that the application can scale to meet the needs of its growing user base. Which of the following solutions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda to process the images. Store the images and metadata in DynamoDB.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to process and store the images with their metadata.
Use AWS Lambda to process the images. Store the images in Amazon S3. Retain DynamoDB to store the image metadata.
Increase the number of EC2 instances to three. Use provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volumes for the storage of images and metadata.

explanations.A: Using Lambda while storing both images and metadata in DynamoDB correctly identifies Lambda as scalable, but storing images directly in DynamoDB is incorrect — DynamoDB is designed for small, predictable data sizes up to 400KB per item, not large binary objects like photos.
explanations.B: Using Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for real-time data streaming and delivery — it's not suitable for image processing or as primary storage for photos and metadata.
explanations.C: This is the correct and best-fit solution: use AWS Lambda to process the images, store the images in Amazon S3, and keep DynamoDB for the image metadata. Lambda auto-scales for highly variable concurrent users, S3 is ideal for large binary objects, and DynamoDB fits small structured metadata.
explanations.D: Scaling to 3 EC2 instances with io2 EBS volumes provides some added capacity but still requires manual management and doesn't provide serverless-level scalability for widely varying, unpredictable traffic.

summary: This is about improving the scalability of an image-processing application with highly variable traffic. The current single-EC2-instance design is a scalability bottleneck.

question: A solutions architect must design a solution that uses Amazon CloudFront with an Amazon S3 origin to store a static website. The company's security policy requires that all website traffic be inspected by AWS WAF. How should the solutions architect comply with these requirements?

options.text: Configure an S3 bucket policy that accepts requests only from the AWS WAF ARN.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward all incoming requests to AWS WAF before requesting content from the S3 origin.
Configure a security group that allows only CloudFront's IP addresses to access the S3 bucket. Attach AWS WAF to CloudFront.
Configure CloudFront and Amazon S3 to use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict access to the S3 bucket. Enable AWS WAF on the distribution.

explanations.A: An S3 bucket policy accepting requests only from the AWS WAF ARN is wrong. AWS WAF is a firewall that inspects requests before they reach CloudFront and has no ARN that can be used this way in a bucket policy.
explanations.B: Having CloudFront forward requests to WAF before requesting content from S3 is architecturally incorrect. WAF attaches to a CloudFront distribution to inspect traffic as it arrives — it isn't a separate destination that CloudFront redirects requests to.
explanations.C: Using a security group to allow only CloudFront's IPs is also incorrect. S3 is not a VPC service, so you cannot apply a security group to it directly.
explanations.D: This is the correct and most secure solution: configure CloudFront and S3 to use an origin access identity (OAI) to restrict access to the S3 bucket, and enable AWS WAF on the distribution. An OAI is a special CloudFront-only identity; the S3 bucket policy allows access only through this identity, preventing bypass via the public S3 URL, and WAF on the distribution inspects all incoming traffic.

summary: This is about securely configuring a static website hosted on S3 and served through CloudFront, while meeting a requirement that all traffic be inspected by AWS WAF.

question: A company's photo-hosting website lets users around the world upload, view, and download photos from their mobile devices. The company currently hosts the static website in an Amazon S3 bucket. Because of the site's growing popularity, its performance has decreased. Users have reported latency issues while uploading and downloading photos. The company must improve the site's performance. Which solution meets these requirements with the least implementation effort?

options.text: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the S3 bucket to improve download performance. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to improve upload performance.

Configure appropriately sized Amazon EC2 instances in multiple AWS Regions. Migrate the application to the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic evenly across the EC2 instances. Configure AWS Global Accelerator to meet the global demand with low latency.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 bucket as an origin to improve download performance. Configure the application to use CloudFront for photo uploads to improve upload performance. Create S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication rules to replicate user data based on location. Redirect downloads to the S3 bucket closest to each user's location.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket to improve network performance. Create an application endpoint to use Global Accelerator instead of the S3 bucket.

explanations.A: This is the correct solution: configure a CloudFront distribution for downloads and enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for uploads. CloudFront caches content at edge locations, dramatically reducing download latency. S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront's edge locations to optimize the upload path to S3. Both are simple toggles on an existing bucket, requiring very little effort for a big performance improvement.
explanations.B: Migrating to multi-Region EC2 with an ALB and Global Accelerator is a highly complex re-architecture of the entire application — far more implementation effort than the requirement calls for.
explanations.C: Using CloudFront for downloads plus multi-Region S3 with Cross-Region Replication and custom redirect logic is far more complex to build and maintain than simply enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration for uploads.
explanations.D: Using Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket is incorrect. Global Accelerator improves TCP/UDP traffic performance to application endpoints; it isn't designed to directly accelerate static content delivery from S3.

summary: This is about improving overall performance for a static website hosted on S3, focusing on latency for both downloads and uploads, with the least implementation effort.

question: A global company uses Amazon API Gateway to design REST APIs for its loyalty program users in the us-east-1 Region and the ap-southeast-2 Region. A solutions architect must design a solution to protect these API Gateway REST APIs, managed by API Gateway across multiple accounts, from SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks. Which solution will meet these requirements with the least amount of administrative effort?

options.text: Set up AWS WAF in both Regions. Associate the regional web ACL with the API stage.
Set up AWS Firewall Manager in both Regions. Centrally configure AWS WAF rules.
Set up AWS Shield in one Region. Associate the regional web ACL with the API stage.
Set up AWS Shield in one Region. Associate the regional web ACLs with the API stage.

explanations.A: Setting up AWS WAF individually in each Region requires separate, repeated configuration for each account and Region — manual and time-consuming at scale, which fails the least-administrative-effort requirement.
explanations.B: This is the correct solution: set up AWS Firewall Manager in both Regions and centrally configure AWS WAF rules. Firewall Manager lets you configure and manage firewall rules centrally across multiple accounts and resources, deploying one set of WAF rules everywhere at once.
explanations.C: Using AWS Shield here is incorrect. AWS Shield is a managed DDoS protection service; its primary purpose isn't application-layer vulnerabilities like SQL injection or XSS. It's also set up in only one Region, but API Gateway APIs are regional, so protection is needed in both Regions.
explanations.D: This has the same problems as the other Shield option: Shield protects against DDoS, not SQL injection or XSS, and setting it up in only one Region leaves the API in the other Region unprotected.

summary: This is about protecting APIs from common web vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS in a multi-Region, multi-account environment, with the least administrative effort.

question: A solutions architect is optimizing a website for an upcoming musical event. Live-streaming footage of the shows will be broadcast in real time, then will be made available on demand. The event is expected to attract a global online audience. Which service will improve performance for both live-streaming and on-demand viewing?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon Route 53
S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanations.A: Amazon CloudFront is the correct service. CloudFront is a global CDN built to accelerate delivery of web content, including video, by caching video files at edge locations worldwide and supporting live video streaming with fast global access.
explanations.B: AWS Global Accelerator improves TCP/UDP traffic to application endpoints, but it doesn't cache content, which is core to improving on-demand streaming performance.
explanations.C: Amazon Route 53 is DNS routing — it directs users to the right endpoint but doesn't directly improve streaming performance itself.
explanations.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration only speeds up uploads to S3 — it doesn't help with downloading or streaming content to end viewers.

summary: This is about optimizing the delivery of video content to a global audience for both live streaming and on-demand viewing, with low latency.

question: A solutions architect needs to help a company optimize the cost of running an application on AWS. The application will use Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda for compute within the architecture. The EC2 instances will run the application's data ingestion layer. Usage of the EC2 instances will be intermittent and unpredictable. Workloads that run on the EC2 instances can be interrupted at any time. The application's front end will run on Fargate, and Lambda will serve the API layer. Usage of the front end and the API layer will be predictable over the next year. Which combination of purchasing options will provide the most cost-effective solution for hosting this application?

options.text: Use Spot Instances for the data ingestion layer.
Use On-Demand Instances for the data ingestion layer.
Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.
Purchase 1-year Reserved Instances for all EC2 instances of the data ingestion layer.
Purchase a 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.

explanations.A: This is correct: Spot Instances are the right fit for the EC2-based data ingestion layer, since that workload is explicitly intermittent, unpredictable, and tolerant of interruption — exactly what Spot Instances are for, at a steep discount versus On-Demand.
explanations.B: On-Demand Instances would technically work for the ingestion layer, but they're needlessly expensive when the workload's interruption-tolerant, unpredictable nature makes it a perfect fit for much cheaper Spot Instances.
explanations.C: This is correct: a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end (Fargate) and API layer (Lambda) is the right purchase, because a Compute Savings Plan is the one purchase option flexible enough to apply across EC2, Fargate, AND Lambda usage — matching the predictable usage of both of those layers under one commitment.
explanations.D: 1-year Reserved Instances for the ingestion layer are wrong on two counts: RIs suit steady, predictable usage, not this unpredictable, interruptible workload, and RIs only cover EC2 — they wouldn't help with Fargate or Lambda anyway.
explanations.E: A 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the front end and API layer is too narrow — it only covers EC2 usage, but that layer actually runs on Fargate and Lambda, which an EC2 Instance Savings Plan wouldn't discount at all.

summary: This question is about matching AWS compute purchasing options to two very different usage patterns in one architecture — an intermittent, interruptible EC2 workload versus a predictable workload spread across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda — to minimize cost.

question: A company has a data-ingestion workflow that consists of the following: - An Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that receives notifications about new data deliveries - An AWS Lambda function that processes and stores the data The ingestion workflow occasionally fails because of network connectivity issues. When failure occurs, the corresponding data is not ingested unless the company manually reruns the job. What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all notifications are eventually processed?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function for deployment across multiple Availability Zones.
Modify the Lambda function's configuration to increase the CPU and memory allocated to the function.
Configure the SNS topic's retry strategy to increase both the number of retries and the wait time between retries.
Configure an Amazon SQS queue as the destination for failed invocations. Modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue.

explanations.A: Configuring Lambda for multi-AZ deployment is a non-issue — Lambda is already highly available by design and runs across multiple AZs automatically, so this doesn't address the failure being described.
explanations.B: Increasing CPU and memory might improve performance for compute-heavy workloads, but it won't solve intermittent network connectivity disruptions, which is the actual cause of the failures here.
explanations.C: Increasing SNS's retry count and wait time doesn't help — that retry policy addresses delivery issues to the destination endpoint, not failures happening during the Lambda function's own execution. Lambda has its own separate retry behavior and simply drops the message if all of its retries fail.
explanations.D: This is the correct solution: configure an SQS queue as the destination for failed invocations, and modify the Lambda function to process messages in the queue. Lambda's "destinations" feature routes failed asynchronous invocations (after retries are exhausted) to SQS automatically, so nothing is lost and the data can still be processed.

summary: This is about making an event-driven workflow more resilient to transient failures. The current setup, triggering a Lambda function via SNS, fails because of network issues, resulting in lost messages.

question: A company runs multiple workloads on virtual machines (VMs) in an on-premises data center. The company is rapidly expanding, but the on-premises data center is unable to scale fast enough to meet business needs. The company wants to move workloads to AWS. Migration is time sensitive, and the company wants to use a lift-and-shift strategy for non-critical workloads. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to gather data about the VMs.
Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN); install replication agent on VMs.
Complete initial replication; run test instances for acceptance testing.
Stop all VM processes; launch the cutover instance.
Use AWS App2Container (A2C) to gather data about the VMs.
Use AWS DMS to migrate the VMs.

explanations.A: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) is used to convert database schemas from one database engine to another and to assess database migration compatibility — it's a database migration tool, not a fit for migrating whole VMs, so it's the wrong tool entirely for this lift-and-shift.
explanations.B: This is the correct first step: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is AWS's purpose-built lift-and-shift (rehost) service. Installing the MGN replication agent on the source VMs starts continuous, block-level replication of the servers into AWS — the foundational step for migrating the non-critical workloads with minimal downtime and without re-architecting them.
explanations.C: This is the correct second step: once the MGN replication agent has completed its initial replication, you launch test instances from the replicated data to run acceptance testing — validating the migrated workload works correctly in AWS before committing to the final cutover.
explanations.D: This is the correct third and final step: once testing passes, you stop processes on the source on-premises VMs and launch the final cutover instance in AWS, completing the migration.
explanations.E: AWS App2Container (A2C) is used to containerize existing Java and .NET applications so they can run on ECS, EKS, or Fargate. That's a different migration strategy (containerization) than a straightforward VM lift-and-shift, so it's the wrong tool here.
explanations.F: AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) is, again, specifically for migrating databases — not for migrating whole virtual machines — so it doesn't fit this lift-and-shift scenario either.

summary: This question is about the correct end-to-end sequence for a lift-and-shift (rehost) migration of on-premises VM-based workloads to AWS using AWS Application Migration Service: install the replication agent, test the replicated instances, then cut over.

question: A security team wants to limit access to specific services or actions in all of the team's AWS accounts. All accounts belong to a large organization in AWS Organizations. The solution must be scalable and there must be a single point where permissions are administered. What should a solutions architect do to accomplish this?

options.text: Create an access control list (ACL) to provide access to the services or actions.
Create an IAM policy that allows the accounts, and attach the policy to a user group.
Create cross-account roles in each account to deny access to the services or actions.
Create a service control policy (SCP) in the root organizational unit to deny access to the services or actions.

explanations.A: Access control lists (ACLs) filter network traffic; they aren't a mechanism for managing IAM- or API-level service and action permissions, so they don't fit this requirement.
explanations.B: An IAM policy attached to a user group can only grant or deny permissions to identities within a single account — it doesn't provide a way to enforce restrictions centrally across every account in the organization, so it fails the requirement for a single point of administration org-wide.
explanations.C: Creating cross-account roles in each account fails the scalability requirement — it's a highly manual process, repeated per account, without a single point of central management.
explanations.D: This is the correct and best-fit solution: a service control policy (SCP) in the root organizational unit. SCPs let you centrally manage permissions for all accounts by attaching a policy to the root OU, denying access to specific services or actions across every account in the organization at once.

summary: This is about centrally managing security permissions across a large number of AWS accounts within an AWS Organization. The key requirements are scalability and a single point of administration.

question: A company needs to retain critical application log files for a long time. The application generates more than 10 TB of log files a month. The company needs to run occasional queries on this data with the ability to query the last month of data more frequently. Data older than 1 month is rarely queried. Which storage option meets these requirements in the most cost-effective way?

options.text: Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanations.A: Storing logs in S3 and using AWS Backup to move them isn't the optimal solution — AWS Backup is designed for broader backup and restore scenarios, not specifically for S3 storage-class lifecycle cost optimization.
explanations.B: This is the optimal and most cost-effective solution: store logs in Amazon S3, and use an S3 Lifecycle policy to move logs older than 1 month to S3 Glacier Deep Archive. S3 Standard handles the frequently-accessed first month; the Lifecycle policy automatically moves older data to the extremely low-cost Glacier Deep Archive class.
explanations.C: Storing logs in CloudWatch Logs is much more expensive for long-term, large-scale storage compared to S3, and pairing it with AWS Backup doesn't change that cost profile.
explanations.D: Storing logs in CloudWatch Logs is expensive at this scale, and S3 Lifecycle policies can't apply directly to CloudWatch Logs storage anyway — they only govern objects already in S3.

summary: This is a classic data-lifecycle-management problem: storing a huge amount of log data for a long time, but with different access patterns over that time, while keeping costs as low as possible.

question: A medical records company is hosting an application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes customer data files that are stored on Amazon S3. The EC2 instances are hosted in public subnets. The EC2 instances access Amazon S3 through the internet, but they do not require any other network access. A new requirement mandates that the network traffic for file transfers follow a private route and is not sent over the internet. What change should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement for the network architecture?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway. Configure the route table for the public subnets to send traffic to Amazon S3 through the NAT gateway.
Configure the security group of the EC2 instances to restrict outbound traffic so that only traffic to the S3 prefix list is allowed.
Move the EC2 instances into private subnets. Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and associate this endpoint with the route table of the private subnets.
Remove the internet gateway from the VPC. Establish an AWS Direct Connect connection, and route traffic to Amazon S3 through this Direct Connect connection.

explanations.A: Creating a NAT gateway is wrong — the instances are already in a public subnet with an internet gateway, so a NAT gateway is redundant here, and traffic would still route to S3 over the public internet either way.
explanations.B: Restricting outbound traffic via security group doesn't change the network path — even limited to the S3 prefix list, traffic still routes to S3 over the public internet, not a private route.
explanations.C: This is the correct solution: move the EC2 instances into private subnets, and create a VPC endpoint for S3, associated with the private subnet's route table. A VPC endpoint lets you privately connect a VPC to S3 without an internet gateway, NAT device, VPN, or Direct Connect — traffic stays entirely within AWS's private network.
explanations.D: Using Direct Connect is a highly overcomplicated solution — Direct Connect is meant for on-premises-to-AWS connectivity, and it's unrelated to routing traffic privately between an EC2 instance and S3 within AWS.

summary: This is about changing the network architecture so that traffic between EC2 and S3 stays within the AWS network instead of traversing the public internet.

question: A company is concerned about the security of its public web application due to recent web attacks. The application uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB). A solutions architect must reduce the risk of DDoS attacks against the application. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Add an Amazon Inspector agent to the Application Load Balancer.
Configure Amazon Macy to prevent attacks.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced to prevent attacks.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to monitor the Application Load Balancer.

explanations.A: Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities on EC2 instances, containers, and Lambda functions — it's not a DDoS protection tool, and it isn't used directly with an ALB for this purpose.
explanations.B: Amazon Macie discovers and protects sensitive data stored in S3 — it's unrelated to DDoS protection.
explanations.C: This is the correct solution: enable AWS Shield Advanced. All AWS customers get Shield Standard by default (basic protection), but for enhanced protection against sophisticated DDoS attacks on resources like an ALB, Shield Advanced provides always-on detection, automatic mitigations, and cost protection against DDoS-related scaling charges.
explanations.D: Amazon GuardDuty is a monitoring and threat-detection/alerting service, not a direct DDoS mitigation service, so it doesn't reduce the risk of an attack on its own.

summary: This is about protecting a public web application, sitting behind an ALB, from denial-of-service attacks.

question: A company runs its e-commerce application on AWS. Each new order is placed as a message on RabbitMQ that runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance in one Availability Zone. This message is then processed by a different application running on another EC2 instance, which stores the details in a PostgreSQL database running on a third EC2 instance. All EC2 instances are in the same Availability Zone. The company needs to redesign its architecture to provide the highest level of availability with the least amount of operational overhead. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the queue to a redundant pair of active/standby RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create an Auto Scaling group with Multi-AZ EC2 instances for the application that hosts the order-processing service. Create another Auto Scaling group with Multi-AZ EC2 instances for the PostgreSQL database.

Migrate the queue to a redundant pair of active/standby RabbitMQ instances on Amazon MQ. Create an Auto Scaling group with Multi-AZ EC2 instances for the application that hosts the order-processing service. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host RabbitMQ. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the order-processing application. Migrate the database to run on a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

Create a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host RabbitMQ. Create another Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the order-processing application. Create a third Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for EC2 instances that host the PostgreSQL database.

explanations.A: Migrating the queue and app to managed/HA solutions but running the database on EC2 within a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group is wrong on the database side — running PostgreSQL on self-managed EC2 requires manually handling replication, failover, backups, and patching, which adds significant operational overhead.
explanations.B: This is the correct and best-fit solution: migrate to Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers across two AZs, add an Auto Scaling group for the application EC2 instances across two AZs, and migrate the database to a Multi-AZ deployment of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Amazon MQ auto-provisions a redundant broker pair, the Auto Scaling group ensures application-layer high availability, and Multi-AZ RDS provides synchronous replication and automatic failover, all fully managed by AWS.
explanations.C: Using self-managed RabbitMQ on an Auto Scaling group, even paired with Multi-AZ RDS, is incorrect because it continues to rely on self-managed RabbitMQ, which is complex to configure and manage for true high availability.
explanations.D: Running all three components — RabbitMQ, the application, and PostgreSQL — on self-managed EC2 across multiple AZs is the worst option in terms of operational effort, since every layer requires manual HA management.

summary: This question is about improving high availability for an application currently running entirely within a single Availability Zone on self-managed EC2 instances.

question: A company is collecting data on temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure in cities across multiple continents. The average volume of data collected per day across all locations is 500 GB. Each location has a high-speed internet connection. The company's weather forecasting applications are based in a single Region and analyze the data at that location. The company wants to aggregate the data from all these global locations as quickly as possible in the Region where the forecasting applications are based. The solution must minimize operational complexity. Which AWS solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination S3 bucket. Use multipart uploads to directly upload site data to the destination S3 bucket.
Upload the data from each site to an S3 bucket in the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy the objects to the destination S3 bucket. Then remove the data from the source S3 bucket.
Schedule AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized jobs daily to transfer data from each site to the closest Region. Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy the objects to the destination S3 bucket.

Upload the data from each site to an Amazon EC2 instance in the closest Region. Store the data in an Amazon EBS volume. On a scheduled basis, take an EBS snapshot and copy it to the Region that contains the destination S3 bucket. Restore the EBS volume in that Region.

explanations.A: This is the correct solution: enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket, and use multipart uploads to directly upload site data. Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront's edge network onto AWS's fast backbone, reducing latency with minimal implementation effort, and multipart uploads improve throughput and resilience for large daily volumes.
explanations.B: Uploading to nearest regional buckets and then using Cross-Region Replication adds unnecessary complexity, cost, and extra latency compared to uploading directly to the destination bucket with Transfer Acceleration.
explanations.C: Using AWS Snowball Edge devices is incorrect here — Snowball Edge is designed for offline transfer or petabyte-scale/no-internet scenarios, and is overkill for 500GB/day when each site already has a high-speed internet connection.
explanations.D: Uploading to EC2 plus EBS and then periodically snapshotting and copying is highly complex and inefficient compared to uploading directly to S3 with Transfer Acceleration.

summary: This is about transferring large amounts of data quickly and easily from multiple global locations into a single S3 bucket. The key constraints are speed, low operational complexity, and existing high-speed internet.

question: A company runs a multi-site web application in an on-premises data center. The application is containerized and runs on a number of Linux servers that connect to a PostgreSQL database that contains user records. The company's growth is hindered by the operational costs of maintaining the infrastructure and capacity planning. A solutions architect must improve the application's infrastructure. What set of actions should the solutions architect take to accomplish this?

options.text: Migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora.
Migrate the web application to be hosted on Amazon EC2 instances.
Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the web application content.
Set up Amazon ElastiCache between the web application and the PostgreSQL database.
Migrate the web application to be hosted on AWS Fargate using Amazon ECS.

explanations.A: This is correct: migrate the self-managed PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora, offloading updates, backups, patching, and scaling to AWS instead of managing them on self-hosted servers.
explanations.B: Migrating the web app to plain EC2 instances just relocates the exact server-management burden the company is trying to eliminate — it still requires provisioning, patching, and capacity planning for servers.
explanations.C: Setting up a CloudFront distribution improves content delivery performance for end users, but it doesn't address the underlying problem of operational overhead from managing infrastructure and capacity planning.
explanations.D: Setting up ElastiCache between the app and the database is a performance optimization for database read load — it's not a fix for the operational overhead of managing servers and capacity.
explanations.E: This is correct: migrate the already-containerized web application to run on AWS Fargate with Amazon ECS. Fargate is serverless container compute, which removes the need to provision, patch, or capacity-plan the underlying servers entirely.

summary: This question is about modernizing a containerized, on-premises web application and its self-managed PostgreSQL database to reduce operational overhead from infrastructure management and capacity planning, by moving each component to the AWS managed service best suited to it.

question: A company is preparing to store confidential data in Amazon S3. For compliance reasons, the data must be encrypted at rest. Encryption key usage must be logged for auditing purposes. Keys must be rotated every year. Which solution meets these requirements and is the most operationally efficient?

options.text: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) with manual rotation
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) with automatic rotation

explanations.A: SSE-C places the responsibility of key management, including rotation and logging, entirely on the customer — highly operationally inefficient, and there's no automatic CloudTrail logging of key usage.
explanations.B: SSE-S3 is simple to use, but key usage isn't logged to CloudTrail since AWS manages the keys entirely internally — this fails the auditing requirement.
explanations.C: SSE-KMS with manual rotation meets the logging requirement (KMS API calls are logged to CloudTrail), but it fails the operational-efficiency requirement, since manual rotation requires creating new keys and re-encrypting data by hand each year.
explanations.D: This is the correct and most suitable solution: SSE-KMS with automatic rotation. All KMS API calls are automatically logged to CloudTrail, and AWS KMS can be configured to automatically rotate customer-managed keys once a year — meeting all requirements with the least operational effort.

summary: This is about choosing the appropriate S3 encryption option for encryption at rest, key-usage audit logging, and annual key rotation, with the least operational effort.

question: A company is migrating its on-premises PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The on-premises database must remain online and available during the migration. The Aurora database must remain synchronized with the on-premises database. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS DMS continuous replication task.
Create a backup of the on-premises database.
Create an AWS DMS replication instance.
Convert the database schema by using the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).
Create a rule in Amazon EventBridge or Amazon CloudWatch Events to monitor database synchronization.

explanations.A: Creating an AWS DMS continuous replication task (CDC) is necessary to keep the target Aurora database synchronized with ongoing changes on the source on-premises database, enabling a zero-downtime migration.
explanations.B: A plain backup of the on-premises database only supports a one-time, offline migration — it doesn't keep the target continuously synchronized with an online source database, so it doesn't meet the requirement to stay in sync during migration.
explanations.C: An AWS DMS replication instance is the compute resource that actually runs any DMS task, including the continuous replication task needed here — it's required to perform the migration and ongoing synchronization.
explanations.D: The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) is used to convert schemas between different database engines. This is a homogeneous migration (PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL), so the schemas already match and SCT isn't needed.
explanations.E: An EventBridge or CloudWatch Events rule to monitor synchronization is a nice-to-have for visibility, but it isn't an essential action for actually performing and maintaining the synchronized migration.

summary: This question is about migrating a database to Aurora PostgreSQL with zero downtime, which requires AWS DMS for continuous, ongoing replication (CDC) rather than a one-time cutover.

question: A company runs a stateless web application in a production environment on a fleet of On-Demand Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences heavy usage during an 8-hour period each business day. Application usage is moderate and steady overnight. Application usage is low during the weekend. The company wants to reduce its EC2 costs without affecting the availability of the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Spot Instances for the entire workload.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot Instances for any additional capacity the application needs.
Use On-Demand Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot Instances for any additional capacity the application needs.
Use Dedicated Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use On-Demand Instances for any additional capacity the application needs.

explanations.A: Using Spot Instances for the entire workload is risky because Spot Instances can be interrupted at any time, which would jeopardize availability for the steady baseline load the application needs to serve every day.
explanations.B: Reserved Instances for the baseline usage give the best discount for the predictable, steady overnight/baseline load, and Spot Instances cost-effectively cover the additional capacity needed during the 8-hour daily spike — since the application is stateless, it tolerates Spot interruptions well. This combination reduces cost without affecting availability.
explanations.C: Using On-Demand Instances for the baseline usage is not the most cost-effective choice — a predictable, steady workload like the overnight baseline is better served by Reserved Instances, which offer a significant discount over On-Demand pricing for committed usage.
explanations.D: Dedicated Instances are the most expensive EC2 purchasing option and exist to satisfy compliance or licensing requirements that isolate hardware — nothing in the scenario calls for that, so this is not cost-effective.

summary: This is about matching EC2 purchasing options to a workload with a predictable steady baseline plus a variable daily spike — Reserved Instances for the baseline and Spot Instances for the burst is the standard cost-optimization pattern.

question: A company runs an online transaction processing (OLTP) workload on AWS. This workload uses an unencrypted Amazon RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. Daily snapshots of the database instance are taken from this instance. What should a solutions architect do to ensure the database and its snapshots are always encrypted moving forward?

options.text: Create a copy of the latest DB snapshot. Encrypt the copy. Replace the existing DB instance by restoring from the encrypted snapshot.
Create a new Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume that is encrypted. Copy the snapshots to the new EBS volume. Enable encryption on the DB instance.
Copy the snapshots and enable encryption using AWS KMS. Restore the encrypted snapshot to the existing DB instance.
Copy the snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket that is encrypted with server-side encryption using AWS KMS (SSE-KMS).

explanations.A: Since encryption status is fixed at instance-creation time, you cannot enable encryption on an existing RDS instance. The supported procedure is to create a copy of the latest snapshot, encrypt that copy, and then restore a new DB instance from the encrypted snapshot, replacing the existing one.
explanations.B: You cannot manually create an encrypted EBS volume and copy RDS snapshots onto it — RDS manages its own internal EBS-backed storage, and this storage cannot be swapped out this way.
explanations.C: Restoring a snapshot always creates a brand-new DB instance; it can never update or replace the storage of an existing DB instance in place. So copying and encrypting snapshots and then 'restoring to the existing instance' isn't something RDS supports.
explanations.D: RDS snapshots are not S3 objects and cannot be directly copied into an S3 bucket, encrypted or otherwise, so this approach isn't valid for encrypting the database.

summary: This question tests the AWS-documented procedure for retroactively encrypting an unencrypted RDS instance and its snapshots — since encryption can't be turned on for an existing instance, you must encrypt a snapshot copy and restore a new instance from it.

question: A company sells ringtones created from clips of popular songs. The files containing the ringtones are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are infrequent for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to save money on storage while keeping the most accessed files readily available for its users. What action should the company take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) as the default storage tier for the objects.
Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a lower-cost storage tier after 90 days.
Configure S3 Inventory to manage the objects and move them to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days.
Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days.

explanations.A: Setting S3 Standard-IA as the default storage tier for all objects is wrong because files are frequently downloaded during their first 90 days, and Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee — applying it from the start would make those frequent early downloads expensive.
explanations.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for objects with unknown or changing access patterns, where it automatically monitors usage and moves objects between tiers. Here, the access pattern (frequent for 90 days, then infrequent) is already known, so Intelligent-Tiering just adds unnecessary monitoring fees without benefit.
explanations.C: S3 Inventory is a reporting tool that lists objects and their metadata — it does not move or transition objects between storage classes, so on its own it cannot fulfill the requirement to shift older files to cheaper storage.
explanations.D: An S3 Lifecycle policy that transitions objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after exactly 90 days directly matches the known access pattern: files stay in the more expensive but retrieval-fee-free Standard tier while frequently accessed, then automatically move to the cheaper Standard-IA tier once downloads become infrequent — the simplest and most cost-effective option.

summary: This question is about choosing the right S3 storage-cost optimization tool for a known, predictable access pattern — a Lifecycle policy with a fixed transition date, rather than Intelligent-Tiering (for unknown patterns) or Inventory (which doesn't move data).

question: A company has a highly dynamic batch processing job that uses many Amazon EC2 instances to complete. The job is stateless in nature, can be started and stopped at any time with no negative impact, and typically takes more than 60 minutes to complete overall. The company has asked a solutions architect to design a scalable and cost-effective solution that meets the requirements of the job. What should the solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Implement EC2 Spot Instances.
Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances.
Implement On-Demand EC2 Instances.
Implement the processing on AWS Lambda.

explanations.A: EC2 Spot Instances can be up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand, and this batch job is stateless, fault-tolerant, and can be freely started and stopped, which is exactly the profile of workload that benefits from Spot's cost savings despite the risk of interruption.
explanations.B: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment and are meant for steady, predictable, long-running workloads. This job is described as 'highly dynamic,' the opposite of the steady usage pattern RIs are optimized for.
explanations.C: On-Demand Instances are the most expensive standard purchasing option, and since a cheaper option (Spot) fits this interruption-tolerant workload perfectly, On-Demand isn't the most cost-effective choice.
explanations.D: AWS Lambda has a hard maximum execution duration of 15 minutes per invocation. This job typically takes more than 60 minutes to complete, which disqualifies Lambda outright regardless of cost.

summary: This question tests matching an EC2 purchasing option to a stateless, interruptible batch workload with no fixed duration commitment — Spot Instances are the standard fit for this profile.

question: An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The instances run in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application performs best when the CPU utilization of the EC2 instances is at or near 40%. What should a solutions architect do to maintain the desired performance level across all instances in the group?

options.text: Use a simple scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
Use a target tracking scaling policy to dynamically scale the Auto Scaling group.
Use an AWS Lambda function to update the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity.
Use scheduled scaling actions to scale up and scale down the Auto Scaling group.

explanations.A: A simple scaling policy reacts to alarm breaches with a fixed adjustment and then enters a cooldown period — it isn't designed to continuously hold a metric at a specific target value over time.
explanations.B: A target tracking scaling policy lets you specify a target value (here, 40% CPU utilization), and Auto Scaling automatically adds or removes instances as needed to keep the metric at that target continuously — exactly matching the requirement to maintain a specific performance level.
explanations.C: Using a custom Lambda function to update the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity is unnecessarily complex and reinvents functionality that Auto Scaling already provides natively through target tracking policies.
explanations.D: Scheduled scaling actions scale capacity up or down at predictable, known times — they don't respond to real-time metric values, so they can't dynamically maintain a target utilization level as load fluctuates unpredictably.

summary: This question is about choosing the right Auto Scaling policy type for maintaining a specific metric value continuously — target tracking is purpose-built for this, unlike simple/step scaling or scheduled scaling.

question: A global company hosts its web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The web application has static data and dynamic data. The company stores its static data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to improve performance and reduce latency for both the static and dynamic data. The company is using Amazon Route 53 for DNS with its own registered domain name. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket and the ALB as origins. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the ALB as an origin. Create a standard AWS Global Accelerator accelerator with the S3 bucket as an endpoint. Configure Route 53 to route traffic to the CloudFront distribution.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as an origin. Create a standard AWS Global Accelerator accelerator with the ALB and CloudFront distribution as endpoints. Create a custom domain name that points to the accelerator's DNS name. Use the custom domain name as an endpoint for the web application.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the ALB as an origin. Create a standard AWS Global Accelerator accelerator with the S3 bucket as an endpoint. Create two domain names. Point one domain name to the CloudFront distribution for dynamic content. Point the other domain name to the accelerator for static content. Use both domain names for the web application.

explanations.A: A single CloudFront distribution can be configured with both the S3 bucket and the ALB as origins, routing requests to the appropriate origin based on cache behaviors or path patterns (e.g., static asset paths to S3, API paths to the ALB). With Route 53 pointing to this distribution, both static and dynamic content benefit from CloudFront's edge caching and low-latency global delivery — the standard best-practice pattern for mixed content types.
explanations.B: This approach splits the two content types across two separate services — CloudFront for the ALB (dynamic) and a standalone Global Accelerator for the S3 bucket (static) — adding unnecessary complexity. Global Accelerator is a network-layer traffic router, not a caching CDN, so it doesn't improve performance for static S3 content the way CloudFront would.
explanations.C: This creates an unnecessarily complex chain (Global Accelerator routing to both the ALB and a CloudFront distribution, with a separate custom domain), when a single CloudFront distribution with two origins accomplishes the same goal more simply.
explanations.D: Using two separate domain names — one for dynamic content routed through CloudFront and another for static content routed through Global Accelerator — needlessly complicates the architecture and the DNS setup instead of using one CloudFront distribution with multiple origins.

summary: This question is about serving both static (S3) and dynamic (ALB) content with low latency behind a single global entry point — a single CloudFront distribution with multiple origins and Route 53 in front of it is the standard, simplest solution.

question: A company's containerized application runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. The application needs to download security certificates before it can communicate with other business applications. The company wants a highly secure solution to encrypt and decrypt the certificates in near-real time. The solution also needs to store data in highly available storage after the data is encrypted. Which solution will meet these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Create secrets in AWS Secrets Manager for the encrypted certificates. Manually update the certificates as needed. Control access to the data by using fine-grained IAM policies.
Create an AWS Lambda function that uses a Python cryptography library to receive and perform encryption operations. Store the function in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create a customer managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Grant the EC2 role permission to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon S3.

Create a customer managed key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Grant the EC2 role permission to use the KMS key for encryption operations. Store the encrypted data on Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.

explanations.A: AWS Secrets Manager is designed for storing and rotating secrets like credentials, not for performing near-real-time encryption/decryption operations on data. Manually updating certificates as needed also fails to meet the 'near-real-time' requirement and adds operational overhead.
explanations.B: Building a custom AWS Lambda function with a Python cryptography library to perform encryption is a self-built, high-maintenance solution — it requires the company to manage the encryption code and library themselves, which is exactly the operational overhead the requirement is trying to avoid.
explanations.C: A customer-managed KMS key lets the EC2 instance's IAM role call the KMS API to encrypt and decrypt data near-real-time with minimal setup, and storing the encrypted data in Amazon S3 provides highly available, durable storage — meeting both the encryption and high-availability requirements with the least operational overhead.
explanations.D: Storing the encrypted data on Amazon EBS volumes is wrong because EBS volumes attach to a single EC2 instance at a time and are tied to a single Availability Zone — they don't provide the highly available, shared storage the requirement calls for, unlike Amazon S3.

summary: This question is about achieving low-overhead, near-real-time encryption backed by highly available storage — a customer-managed AWS KMS key combined with Amazon S3 storage is the managed-service fit, versus self-built or single-AZ alternatives.

question: A company recently migrated its message-processing system to AWS. The system receives messages into an ActiveMQ queue running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Messages are processed by a consumer application running on Amazon EC2. The consumer application processes the messages and writes results to a MySQL database running on Amazon EC2. The company wants this application to be highly available with low operational complexity. Which architecture offers the highest availability?

options.text: Add a second ActiveMQ server to another Availability Zone. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone. Back up the MySQL database to an additional Availability Zone.

Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone. Back up the MySQL database to an additional Availability Zone.

Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an additional consumer EC2 instance in another Availability Zone. Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ enabled.

Use Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers configured across two Availability Zones. Add an Auto Scaling group for the consumer EC2 instances across two Availability Zones. Use Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ enabled.
