explanations.A: Manually running a second self-managed ActiveMQ server, an extra consumer instance, and backing up MySQL on EC2 to another AZ still leaves every layer self-managed — this is complex, error-prone, and doesn't offload operational burden the way managed services would.
explanations.B: Migrating to Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers addresses the queue layer, and adding a consumer instance in another AZ helps availability, but backing up the MySQL database on EC2 (rather than using a managed database service) still leaves the database tier self-managed and less resilient.
explanations.C: This option upgrades the queue to Amazon MQ and the database to Multi-AZ RDS, both good choices, but the consumer tier only gets a single additional static EC2 instance rather than an Auto Scaling group — it lacks the automatic scaling and self-healing that a true highly available consumer tier needs.
explanations.D: This is the most comprehensive solution: Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers across two AZs replaces the self-managed ActiveMQ server with a managed, highly available message broker; an Auto Scaling group for the consumer EC2 instances across two AZs ensures the processing tier can scale and self-heal; and Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ enabled provides a managed, highly available database. Every layer is upgraded to its fully managed, HA equivalent.

summary: This question is about achieving high availability with low operational complexity across all three tiers of a message-processing system — the correct answer replaces every self-managed component (broker, consumer fleet, database) with its fully managed, multi-AZ equivalent.

question: A company hosts a website analytics application on a single On-Demand Amazon EC2 instance. The analytics software is written in PHP and uses a MySQL database. The analytics software, the web server that runs the software, and the database server all run on the same EC2 instance. The application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly. Which of the following solutions will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second On-Demand EC2 instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load across each EC2 instance.

Migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second On-Demand EC2 instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across each EC2 instance.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL instance. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization exceeds 75%.

Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group by using the launch template. Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.

explanations.A: Migrating the database to RDS is a good step, but adding just one extra On-Demand instance behind an ALB provides only a single fixed increment of capacity, not true auto-scaling — it won't scale seamlessly as load changes.
explanations.B: Similar to option A, this migrates the database to RDS and adds one static extra instance, but distributes traffic using Route 53 weighted routing instead of a proper load balancer — weighted routing isn't the best-practice tool for distributing application load across instances, and this still isn't real auto-scaling.
explanations.C: Using a Lambda function triggered by a CloudWatch alarm to stop the EC2 instance and change its instance type causes downtime while the instance is stopped and resized — this doesn't provide seamless scaling, since the application becomes unavailable during the resize.
explanations.D: Migrating the database to Aurora MySQL removes the database as a single point of failure and a manual-management burden; creating an AMI and launch template, then an Auto Scaling group with a Spot Fleet, provides true seamless scaling as demand changes while keeping costs low (since the app is stateless and can tolerate Spot interruptions); attaching an ALB distributes traffic across the scaling fleet. This is the most complete and cost-effective solution.

summary: This question is about moving a single-instance monolithic app to a properly scalable, cost-effective architecture — the correct answer separates the database onto a managed service and uses a true Auto Scaling group (with Spot Fleet for cost savings) behind a load balancer, rather than adding a single static extra instance.

question: A company wants to build a scalable key management infrastructure to support developers who need to use encryption in their applications. What should a solutions architect do to reduce the operational burden?

options.text: Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to protect the encryption keys.
Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to protect the encryption keys.
Use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to create, store, and assign the encryption keys.
Use an IAM policy to limit the scope of users who have access permissions to protect the encryption keys.

explanations.A: Multi-factor authentication protects user sign-in credentials — it has nothing to do with creating, storing, or managing the lifecycle of encryption keys themselves.
explanations.B: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is a fully managed service purpose-built for creating, storing, rotating, and auditing encryption keys at scale, which directly reduces the operational burden of building and maintaining a key management infrastructure.
explanations.C: AWS Certificate Manager is designed for provisioning, managing, and deploying SSL/TLS certificates — it is not a general-purpose encryption key management service for application-level encryption.
explanations.D: An IAM policy can restrict who has permission to access encryption keys, but on its own it doesn't create, store, rotate, or manage keys — it only controls access, so it doesn't address the operational burden of running key management infrastructure.

summary: This question is about choosing a managed service to reduce the operational burden of building encryption key management infrastructure — AWS KMS is purpose-built for exactly this, unlike MFA, ACM, or IAM policies alone.

question: A company hosts a data lake on AWS. The data lake consists of data in Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The company needs a reporting solution that provides data visualization and includes all the data sources within the data lake. Only the company's management team should have full access to all the visualizations. The rest of the company should have only limited access. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate IAM roles.
Create an analysis in Amazon QuickSight. Connect all the data sources and create new datasets. Publish dashboards to visualize the data. Share the dashboards with the appropriate users and groups.

Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Create an AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) job to produce reports. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.

Create an AWS Glue table and crawler for the data in Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena Federated Query to access data within Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Generate reports by using Amazon Athena. Publish the reports to Amazon S3. Use S3 bucket policies to limit access to the reports.

explanations.A: QuickSight dashboards are shared using QuickSight's own users and groups model, not IAM roles — sharing 'with the appropriate IAM roles' isn't how QuickSight access control works, so this option describes an invalid sharing mechanism.
explanations.B: Creating an analysis in QuickSight, connecting all the data sources (S3 and RDS for PostgreSQL) to build datasets, publishing dashboards, and sharing those dashboards with the appropriate QuickSight users and groups meets the requirement for interactive data visualization across all data lake sources, while natively supporting tiered access — the management team can be given full access and everyone else limited access through QuickSight's built-in sharing permissions.
explanations.C: An AWS Glue crawler and ETL job can process and produce reports, but this is a data-processing/ETL pipeline, not an interactive data-visualization tool — it doesn't provide dashboards, and restricting access via S3 bucket policies is a coarser, less flexible access model than QuickSight's user/group sharing.
explanations.D: Using Athena Federated Query to combine S3 and RDS data and then publishing static reports to S3 still results in static reports rather than interactive dashboards, and again relies on S3 bucket policies for access control rather than a purpose-built visualization tool with fine-grained sharing.

summary: This question is about building a reporting/visualization solution across multiple data sources with tiered access levels for different user groups — Amazon QuickSight, with its native users/groups sharing model, is purpose-built for this, unlike ETL-and-static-report approaches.

question: A company runs its media-processing application on premises. The company wants to reduce its storage costs and has already moved all its data to Amazon S3. The on-premises processing application requires low-latency access to the storage. The company needs to design a storage solution for the application. The storage solution must maintain the required application performance. Which storage solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Use an Amazon S3 Mount Point to access the data in Amazon S3 for the on-premises application.
Configure an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Copy the data from Amazon S3 to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Configure an Amazon FSx File Gateway to provide storage for the on-premises application.
Configure an on-premises file server. Use the Amazon S3 API to connect to the S3 storage. Configure the application to access the storage from the on-premises file server.

explanations.A: An S3 Mount Point (Mountpoint for Amazon S3) has no local caching layer for the on-premises application — every file access still has to travel over the internet to S3, so it doesn't solve the low-latency requirement.
explanations.B: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway, deployed on-premises, presents an NFS/SMB file share to the application and caches frequently accessed data locally, giving low-latency access while asynchronously and transparently syncing data with the underlying S3 buckets — the most cost-effective way to bridge on-premises low-latency needs with S3-based storage.
explanations.C: Copying all the S3 data into a new Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system, and additionally configuring an FSx File Gateway, means duplicating the entire dataset into another storage service just to use a gateway — this is unnecessarily expensive and complex compared to simply gatewaying directly to the existing S3 data.
explanations.D: Configuring an on-premises file server to call the S3 API directly is a complex, custom-built integration, and because every request still goes to S3 over the network, it doesn't solve the low-latency access problem either.

summary: This question is about giving an on-premises application low-latency access to data that already lives in S3 — AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway is the purpose-built hybrid solution that caches data locally while keeping S3 as the source of truth.

question: A digital image-processing company wants to migrate its on-premises monolithic application to AWS Cloud. The company processes thousands of images and generates large files as a part of the processing workflow. The company needs a solution to manage the growing number of image-processing jobs. The solution also needs to reduce the manual work of the image-processing workflow. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure of the solution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS).
Use AWS Batch jobs to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon S3.
Use AWS Lambda and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process the images. Store the processed files in Amazon FSx.
Deploy a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances to process the images. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the workflow. Store the processed files in Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS).

explanations.A: Running the processing on ECS with EC2 Spot Instances still requires the company to manage the underlying EC2 fleet (capacity, scaling, patching) — it doesn't meet the 'no infrastructure to manage' requirement, even though SQS can help orchestrate work.
explanations.B: AWS Batch is a fully managed service that provisions and manages the compute needed to run batch jobs without the company managing any servers; AWS Step Functions orchestrates the multi-step image-processing workflow without custom orchestration code; and Amazon S3 provides scalable, cost-effective storage for the large output files. Together these meet the growing-job-volume, reduced-manual-work, and no-infrastructure-management requirements with the least operational overhead.
explanations.C: AWS Lambda has a maximum execution duration of 15 minutes, which is likely insufficient for processing large image files as part of this workflow, and pairing it with EC2 Spot Instances (which do require infrastructure management) undercuts the 'no infrastructure' requirement as well.
explanations.D: Deploying and managing a fleet of EC2 instances directly, even with Step Functions for orchestration, means the company must manage the underlying EC2 infrastructure themselves — the highest operational overhead of the options presented.

summary: This question is about processing a growing volume of image-processing jobs with workflow orchestration and no infrastructure management — AWS Batch plus Step Functions plus S3 is the fully managed combination that fits all three requirements.

question: A company has recently migrated to AWS and wants to implement a solution to protect the traffic that flows in and out of the production VPC. The company had an on-premises solution that was managed by a security team, but this team is not knowledgeable about AWS. The on-premises solution required a review of central rules by a firewall specialist every 4 hours to ensure the correct policies were being applied. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor and filter traffic for the production VPC.
Use Traffic Mirroring to mirror traffic from the production VPC for inspection and filtering.
Use AWS Network Firewall to create the necessary rules for traffic inspection and filtering for the production VPC.
Use AWS Firewall Manager to create the necessary rules for traffic inspection and filtering for the production VPC.

explanations.A: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service — it monitors for malicious activity and generates findings/alerts, but it has no ability to actively block or filter network traffic itself.
explanations.B: VPC Traffic Mirroring copies traffic out of the VPC to a separate inspection target for out-of-band analysis — it doesn't filter or block traffic in the actual data path, so it can't serve as an inline firewall.
explanations.C: AWS Network Firewall is a fully managed, stateful/stateless traffic inspection and filtering service that is deployed directly inside the VPC's traffic path — this is the direct cloud equivalent of the on-premises firewall appliance the security team used to manage, and it lets AWS (not the team) handle the underlying infrastructure and rule engine.
explanations.D: AWS Firewall Manager is a central management tool for administering firewall rules and policies across multiple accounts and other firewall services (like Network Firewall or WAF) — it is not itself a firewall that performs traffic inspection, so on its own it doesn't filter production VPC traffic.

summary: This question is about replacing an on-premises inline traffic-inspection firewall with an AWS-native equivalent that a non-AWS-expert security team can manage — AWS Network Firewall is the actual traffic-filtering service, unlike detection-only or traffic-copying tools.

question: A company is building a containerized application on premises and decides to move the application to AWS. The application will have thousands of users soon after it is deployed. The company does not want to manage the underlying infrastructure to run the container service. The company needs to deploy the containerized application in a highly available architecture that minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Store container images in an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type to run the containers. Use target tracking to scale automatically based on demand.

Store container images in an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Use an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with the Amazon EC2 launch type to run the containers. Use target tracking to scale automatically based on demand.

Store container images in a repository that runs on an Amazon EC2 instance. Run the containers on EC2 instances that are spread across multiple Availability Zones. Monitor the average CPU utilization in Amazon CloudWatch. Launch new EC2 instances as needed.

Create an AMI that contains the container image. Launch EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. Use an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to scale out EC2 instances when the average CPU utilization threshold is exceeded.

explanations.A: Storing images in Amazon ECR and running the containers on an ECS cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type eliminates the need to provision, patch, or scale any underlying EC2 instances — Fargate is serverless container compute. Using target tracking scaling automatically adjusts capacity to demand. This combination meets the high-availability, thousands-of-users, and minimal-operational-overhead requirements.
explanations.B: Using the ECS EC2 launch type still requires the company to provision, patch, and manage the underlying EC2 instances that host the containers — this doesn't minimize operational overhead the way Fargate does, even with target tracking scaling.
explanations.C: Running a self-hosted container image repository and manually monitoring CPU utilization to launch new EC2 instances is the most operationally heavy option — it requires managing both the registry and the compute infrastructure by hand.
explanations.D: Baking the container image into an AMI and running it on an EC2 Auto Scaling group is a poor fit for containerized applications — every application change requires building and deploying a new AMI, which is far more operationally burdensome than using a container orchestration service directly.

summary: This question is about running a containerized application at scale with high availability and minimal infrastructure management — ECS with the Fargate launch type removes EC2 management entirely, unlike the EC2 launch type or AMI-based approaches.

question: A company has a three-tier application that processes customer orders. The web tier consists of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The processing tier consists of EC2 instances. The company has decoupled the web tier and the processing tier by using Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). The storage tier uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. During peak hours, users report delays and stalled order processing. During these delays, the company notices that the EC2 instances that are running the processing tier are at 100% CPU utilization, and the SQS queue is filling up. The peak hours are variable and unpredictable. The company needs to improve the performance of the application. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Implement scheduled scaling for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out the processing tier instances during peak hours. Use CPU utilization as the metric for scaling.
Implement Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the DynamoDB storage tier. Use target utilization as the metric for scaling.
Add an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache the responses for the web tier. Use HTTP latency as the metric for scaling.
Implement a target tracking scaling policy for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out the processing tier instances. Use the ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute to determine when to scale.

explanations.A: Scheduled scaling only works for predictable, known time-based patterns, but the peak hours here are described as variable and unpredictable — a fixed schedule can't adapt to that. It also scales based on CPU utilization, but the real signal of backlog is the growing SQS queue, not just CPU.
explanations.B: Adding Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of DynamoDB targets the storage tier, but the bottleneck described is the processing tier — the EC2 instances running at 100% CPU — not the DynamoDB storage layer, so this doesn't address the actual problem.
explanations.C: Adding a CloudFront distribution to cache web-tier responses targets the wrong tier as well — the web tier handles dynamic order requests, which are generally not well-suited to caching, and the actual bottleneck is in the processing tier, not the web tier.
explanations.D: A target tracking scaling policy for the processing tier's Auto Scaling group, using the SQS queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute as the scaling metric, directly ties the number of processing instances to the actual amount of pending work in the queue. This responds correctly to variable, unpredictable peak hours and directly addresses the observed bottleneck (100% CPU on the processing tier and a growing queue).

summary: This question is about scaling the correct tier in a decoupled, queue-based architecture in response to unpredictable spikes — scaling the processing tier based on the SQS queue depth (not CPU, and not the wrong tier entirely) directly matches the observed bottleneck.

question: A security team wants to limit access to specific services or actions in all of the team's AWS accounts by using AWS Organizations. The company wants to restrict all its accounts to use only the AP-Northeast-3 Region. The company's administrators must not be permitted to connect VPCs to the internet. Which solutions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Control Tower to implement data residency guardrails to deny internet access and deny access to all AWS Regions except AP-Northeast-3.
Use rules in AWS WAF to block internet access. Deny access to all AWS Regions except AP-Northeast-3 in the AWS account settings.
Use AWS Organizations to configure service control policies (SCPs) that prevent VPCs from accessing the internet. Deny access to all AWS Regions except AP-Northeast-3.
Create an outbound rule for the network ACL in each VPC to deny all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. Create an IAM policy for each user to prevent the use of any AWS Region other than AP-Northeast-3.
Use AWS Config to enable managed rules to detect and alert on internet gateways, and to detect and alert on new resources being deployed outside of AP-Northeast-3.

explanations.A: AWS Control Tower's data residency guardrails can be configured to deny internet access to VPCs and deny access to all AWS Regions except an approved one (AP-Northeast-3 here). This is a preventative, centrally managed control that automatically applies across all accounts in the organization.
explanations.B: AWS WAF operates at the web application layer (filtering HTTP requests to protect web applications) — it has no ability to control or block VPC-level internet access, so it's the wrong tool for restricting how VPCs connect to the internet.
explanations.C: AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) can be written to deny actions that would allow VPCs to reach the internet (such as attaching internet gateways) and to deny access to any Region other than AP-Northeast-3. Like Control Tower guardrails, SCPs are preventative controls enforced centrally across every account in the organization, which scales well.
explanations.D: Configuring per-VPC network ACL rules and per-user IAM policies individually across every account does not scale for a large organization — it requires manually replicating configuration everywhere rather than using a centralized, organization-wide control.
explanations.E: AWS Config managed rules can detect and alert when an internet gateway exists or when resources are deployed outside the approved Region, but this is a detective control — it identifies violations after they've already happened, rather than preventing them from occurring in the first place, which is what the requirement calls for.

summary: This question is about enforcing organization-wide, preventative guardrails — restricting Regions and blocking VPC internet access — using AWS Organizations' centrally managed controls (Control Tower guardrails and SCPs) rather than per-account or detective-only approaches.

question: A gaming company is designing a highly available architecture. The application runs on a modified Linux kernel and supports only UDP-based traffic. The company needs the front-end layer to provide the best possible user experience. That layer must have low latency, route traffic to the nearest edge location, and provide static IP addresses for entry into the application endpoints. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon Route 53 to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in an Auto Scaling group.
Configure Amazon CloudFront to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use AWS Lambda for the application in an Auto Scaling group.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator to forward requests to a Network Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an Auto Scaling group.
Configure Amazon API Gateway to forward requests to an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon EC2 instances for the application in an Auto Scaling group.

explanations.A: An Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and does not support UDP traffic, and Lambda functions in an Auto Scaling group is also not a valid combination — this doesn't fit an application that only supports UDP-based traffic.
explanations.B: Amazon CloudFront is an HTTP/HTTPS-only content delivery network — it cannot forward UDP traffic to a Network Load Balancer, so this doesn't work for a UDP-only gaming application.
explanations.C: AWS Global Accelerator operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), provides static anycast IP addresses for entry into the application, and automatically routes traffic to the nearest healthy AWS edge location for low latency. Forwarding to a Network Load Balancer — the only Elastic Load Balancer type that natively supports UDP — with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind it, satisfies all the stated requirements: UDP support, low latency, nearest-edge routing, and static IPs.
explanations.D: Amazon API Gateway is also a Layer 7/HTTP(S)-focused service and doesn't support UDP traffic, making it unsuitable for an application that only communicates over UDP.

summary: This question is about fronting a UDP-only, latency-sensitive application with a front-end layer that supports UDP, routes to the nearest edge, and provides static entry IPs — AWS Global Accelerator paired with a Network Load Balancer is the only combination that satisfies all of Layer 4 support, edge routing, and static IPs.

question: A company runs a two-tier e-commerce website on AWS. The web tier consists of a load balancer that sends traffic to Amazon EC2 instances. The database tier uses an Amazon RDS DB instance. The EC2 instances and the RDS DB instance should not be accessible from the public internet. The EC2 instances need internet access to complete order-payment processing through a third-party web service. The application must be highly available. Which combination of configuration options will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in private subnets. Deploy the RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment in private subnets.
Configure a VPC with two private subnets and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy the Application Load Balancer in the private subnets.
Use an Auto Scaling group to launch the EC2 instances in public subnets across two Availability Zones. Deploy the RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment in private subnets.
Configure a VPC with one public subnet, one private subnet, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy the Application Load Balancer in the public subnet.
Configure a VPC with two public subnets and two private subnets, and two NAT gateways across two Availability Zones. Deploy the Application Load Balancer in the public subnets.

explanations.A: Launching the EC2 instances via an Auto Scaling group in private subnets keeps them inaccessible from the public internet while still allowing scaling across multiple Availability Zones, and deploying the RDS DB instance in a Multi-AZ deployment within private subnets keeps the database private while providing automatic failover for high availability. This addresses the 'not publicly accessible' and 'highly available' requirements for the compute and database tiers.
explanations.B: Deploying the Application Load Balancer in private subnets would make it unreachable from the internet, but the ALB is the public-facing entry point for the e-commerce website's users — it needs to be internet-facing, so putting it in private subnets breaks the application entirely.
explanations.C: Launching the EC2 instances in public subnets violates the requirement that the EC2 instances not be accessible from the public internet directly — instances handling application logic should sit in private subnets behind the load balancer.
explanations.D: A VPC with only one public and one private subnet (even with two NAT gateways) spans only a single Availability Zone for its subnets, which fails the high-availability requirement — a highly available design needs subnets, and therefore resources, spread across at least two AZs.
explanations.E: A VPC configured with two public subnets and two private subnets, along with two NAT gateways, spread across two Availability Zones, provides true high availability at the network level. Deploying the Application Load Balancer in the public subnets keeps it internet-facing (as required for the public-facing web tier) while the EC2 instances and RDS DB instance remain in the private subnets, and the NAT gateways in each AZ give the private EC2 instances outbound internet access (needed for the third-party payment processing) without exposing them directly to inbound internet traffic.

summary: This question is about designing a highly available two-tier VPC architecture where the compute and database tiers are private but still need outbound internet access — the correct combination places the ALB in public subnets and the EC2/RDS resources in private subnets, both spread across two Availability Zones with per-AZ NAT gateways.

question: A company hosts its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system in the us-east-1 Region. The system runs on Amazon EC2 instances. Customers use a public API, also hosted on EC2 instances, to exchange information with the ERP system. International customers are reporting slow response times from the API from their data centers. What solution will improve response times for the international customers MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection with a public virtual interface (VIF) to provide connectivity from each customer's data center to the us-east-1 Region. Route customer API requests using the Direct Connect gateway to the ERP system's API.
Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API. Configure the managed and optimized caching policy to improve caching efficiency.

Set up AWS Global Accelerator. Configure listeners for the necessary ports. Configure endpoint groups for the appropriate Regions to distribute the traffic. Create an endpoint in the group for the API.
Use an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to create dedicated VPN tunnels between the Regions and customer networks. Route traffic to the API over the VPN connections.

explanations.A: Setting up a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection with a public VIF for each customer's data center is expensive to provision and manage per-customer, and doesn't scale for a public API used by many international customers — Direct Connect is meant for consistent, high-volume dedicated connectivity from a single organization's network, not a broad public customer base.
explanations.B: Amazon CloudFront with an optimized caching policy is designed to cache and serve static or semi-static content — but ERP API responses (business data exchanges) are typically dynamic and not cacheable, so caching wouldn't meaningfully improve response times here.
explanations.C: AWS Global Accelerator, configured with listeners and endpoint groups directing traffic to the API's Region, routes each customer's traffic to the nearest AWS edge location and then over AWS's private, optimized global network backbone to the API endpoint — improving response times for all customers without requiring a dedicated connection to be set up per customer, making it the most cost-effective and scalable solution.
explanations.D: Setting up dedicated Site-to-Site VPN tunnels between the Region and every customer's network is not scalable for a public API with many customers, and VPN traffic still travels over the public internet (just encrypted), so it doesn't address the underlying latency issue the way routing over AWS's backbone would.

summary: This question is about improving global API response times for international customers cost-effectively — AWS Global Accelerator routes traffic over AWS's optimized backbone via the nearest edge location, without requiring per-customer dedicated connections like Direct Connect or VPN.

question: A company has workloads running on AWS. The company needs to connect to a service from a third-party provider. This service is hosted in the provider's VPC. According to the company's security team, the connection must be private and must be restricted to the target service. The connection must be initiated only by the company's VPC. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a VPC peering connection between the company's VPC and the provider's VPC. Update the route table to include the target service.
Ask the provider to create a virtual private gateway (VGW) in its VPC. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of the company's VPC. Update the route table to connect to the target service.
Ask the provider to create a VPC endpoint for the target service. Use AWS PrivateLink to connect to the target service.

explanations.A: VPC peering connects two VPCs at the network level and grants routable access between them based on route tables — it doesn't restrict access down to a single specific service, so it's more permissive than the requirement calls for.
explanations.B: A virtual private gateway (VGW) is used to connect a VPC to an on-premises network (or another network) over VPN or Direct Connect — it isn't the mechanism for privately connecting to a specific service running inside another VPC, so this doesn't fit the requirement.
explanations.C: A NAT gateway would route the connection out through a public subnet and over the public internet to reach the provider's service — this violates the requirement that the connection be private, and also isn't restricted to a single target service.
explanations.D: Having the provider create a VPC endpoint for their specific service and using AWS PrivateLink to connect to it restricts the connection to exactly that one service, keeps all traffic on the AWS private network (never touching the public internet), and the connection is initiated from the company's VPC to the endpoint — meeting all three stated requirements: private, restricted to the target service, and company-initiated.

summary: This question is about privately connecting to one specific service in a third-party VPC without broad network access — AWS PrivateLink via a provider-created VPC endpoint is purpose-built to restrict access to a single service, unlike VPC peering, a VGW, or a NAT gateway.

question: A company wants to use a high performance computing (HPC) infrastructure on AWS for financial risk modeling. The company's HPC workloads run on Linux. Each HPC workflow runs on hundreds of Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, is short-lived, and generates thousands of output files that will eventually be stored in a persistent data store for analytics and future reference. The company seeks a cloud storage solution that allows the copying of on-premises data to and from a persistent store that also allows the data to be made available on all Amazon EC2 instances. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with Amazon S3
Amazon S3 Glacier integrated with Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon S3 bucket with a VPC endpoint integrated with a general purpose SSD (gp2) Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume

explanations.A: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system purpose-built for HPC and compute-intensive Linux workloads, and it integrates natively with Amazon S3 to import data from and export data to S3 — allowing on-premises data to be copied to a persistent S3 store while also being available as a shared, high-performance file system across hundreds of EC2 instances running the HPC workflow.
explanations.B: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is built for Windows-based workloads using the SMB protocol — this HPC workload runs on Linux, so it isn't the right file system choice regardless of its S3 integration.
explanations.C: Amazon S3 Glacier is a low-cost archival storage class with slow retrieval times, unsuitable for actively used HPC data, and Amazon EBS volumes attach to only a single EC2 instance at a time — neither is a shared file system that hundreds of instances can access simultaneously.
explanations.D: An S3 bucket accessed via a VPC endpoint, paired with a general-purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume, doesn't provide a shared file system either — gp2 EBS volumes are single-instance-attached, so they can't be made available across hundreds of concurrently running HPC instances.

summary: This question is about providing a shared, high-performance file system for a Linux-based HPC workload that also needs to persist output durably and exchange data with on-premises storage — Amazon FSx for Lustre integrated with S3 is purpose-built for exactly this combination.

question: A company recently started using Amazon Aurora as the data store for its global ecommerce application. When large reports are run, developers report that the ecommerce application is performing poorly. After reviewing metrics in Amazon CloudWatch, a solutions architect finds that the reads IOPS and CPU utilization metrics spike when the monthly reports run. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?

options.text: Migrate the monthly reports to run on Amazon Redshift.
Migrate the monthly reports to run on an Aurora Replica.
Migrate the Aurora database to a larger instance class.
Increase the provisioned IOPS on the Aurora instance.

explanations.A: Migrating the monthly reports to run on Amazon Redshift would require building an entirely new ETL pipeline to move data from Aurora into a separate data warehouse — this is a much larger undertaking than necessary just to isolate report-driven read load from the primary database.
explanations.B: Migrating the monthly reports to run against an Aurora Replica offloads the heavy, read-only reporting queries from the primary Aurora instance onto a separate read replica, preventing the report workload from consuming the IOPS and CPU that the primary instance needs for regular application traffic. Since the replica is only needed while reports run, this is also cost-effective compared to permanently over-provisioning the primary.
explanations.C: Migrating to a larger Aurora instance class would resolve the resource contention, but it means paying for a permanently larger (and more expensive) instance 24/7, even during the vast majority of the time when the monthly reports aren't running — not the most cost-effective option.
explanations.D: Increasing provisioned IOPS doesn't apply to Aurora the way it does to standard RDS engines — Aurora's storage layer is decoupled from compute and automatically scales I/O, so manually increasing 'provisioned IOPS' isn't a meaningful lever here and wouldn't isolate the report workload from the primary anyway.

summary: This question is about cost-effectively isolating a periodic, resource-intensive reporting workload from an Aurora database's primary instance — offloading the reports to an Aurora Read Replica is the standard, pay-only-when-needed solution.

question: A large media company hosts a web application on AWS. The company wants to start caching confidential media files so that users around the world can access the files with low latency. The content is stored in Amazon S3 buckets. The company must deliver the content quickly, regardless of where the requests originate geographically. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy AWS Global Accelerator to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront to connect the S3 buckets to CloudFront edge servers.
Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to connect the S3 buckets to the web application.

explanations.A: AWS DataSync is a service for transferring large amounts of data between on-premises storage and AWS (or between AWS storage services) — it is a data-transfer tool, not a content delivery or caching service, so it doesn't help serve content to end users with low latency.
explanations.B: AWS Global Accelerator improves routing performance by directing traffic over AWS's global network to the optimal endpoint, but it does not cache content — since the requirement is specifically about caching confidential media files for low-latency access, Global Accelerator alone doesn't fulfill it.
explanations.C: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN) purpose-built to cache content — including from an S3 origin — at edge locations distributed around the world, so users anywhere can retrieve cached copies with low latency regardless of where their requests originate. This directly meets the requirement to cache and quickly deliver confidential media files globally.
explanations.D: Amazon Simple Queue Service is a message queuing service used for decoupling application components — it has no role in caching or delivering content to end users, so it's unrelated to this requirement.

summary: This question is about caching and delivering media content with low latency to users worldwide — Amazon CloudFront is the purpose-built CDN for caching content at edge locations close to users, unlike a data-transfer tool, a routing optimizer, or a messaging queue.

question: A company wants to migrate its existing on-premises monolithic application to AWS. The company wants to keep as much of the front-end code and the backend code as possible. However, the company wants to break the application into smaller applications. A different team will manage each application. The company needs a highly scalable solution that minimizes operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Host the application on AWS Lambda. Integrate the application with Amazon API Gateway.
Host the application with AWS Amplify. Connect the application to an Amazon API Gateway API that is integrated with AWS Lambda.
Host the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Set up an Application Load Balancer with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group as targets.
Host the application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). Set up an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS as the target.

explanations.A: Hosting on AWS Lambda integrated with API Gateway is wrong because Lambda requires significant refactoring — its 15-minute execution limit and event-driven model don't fit an existing monolithic codebase, contradicting the requirement to keep as much of the existing code as possible.
explanations.B: AWS Amplify is designed for building new applications from scratch, not for migrating and decomposing an existing on-premises monolith, so it doesn't fit this migration scenario.
explanations.C: Hosting on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer with an Auto Scaling group is essentially a lift-and-shift of the monolith — it doesn't break the application into independently managed microservices, which is a core requirement.
explanations.D: This is correct. Hosting the application on Amazon ECS with an Application Load Balancer targeting ECS lets the company containerize the existing front-end and back-end code with minimal rewriting, while still splitting the application into separate services that different teams can manage independently — providing high scalability with minimal operational overhead.

summary: This question is about migrating and decomposing an existing monolithic application into independently managed pieces while reusing as much existing code as possible and minimizing operational overhead.

question: A company is preparing to deploy a new serverless workload. A solutions architect must use the principle of least privilege to configure permissions that will be used to run an AWS Lambda function. An Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule will invoke the function. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an execution role to the function with lambda:InvokeFunction as the action and * as the principal.
Add an execution role to the function with lambda:InvokeFunction as the action and service lambda.amazonaws.com as the principal.
Add a resource-based policy to the function with lambda:* as the action and service events.amazonaws.com as the principal.
Add a resource-based policy to the function with lambda:InvokeFunction as the action and service events.amazonaws.com as the principal.

explanations.A: Adding an execution role with lambda:InvokeFunction and * as the principal is wrong — an execution role controls what the function itself can do, not who is allowed to invoke it, and using a wildcard principal violates least privilege.
explanations.B: Adding an execution role with lambda:InvokeFunction and the lambda.amazonaws.com service as principal is wrong for the same reason — an execution role doesn't control invocation permissions, and lambda.amazonaws.com isn't the service that needs to invoke this function.
explanations.C: A resource-based policy with lambda:* as the action grants far more permissions than needed (the ability to perform any Lambda action, not just invoke), which violates the principle of least privilege.
explanations.D: This is correct. A resource-based policy on the function granting lambda:InvokeFunction to the events.amazonaws.com service principal is the minimal permission needed to let the EventBridge rule invoke the function, satisfying least privilege.

summary: This question tests understanding of least-privilege permissions for allowing an EventBridge rule to invoke a Lambda function — specifically the distinction between execution roles (what the function can do) and resource-based policies (who can invoke the function).

question: A company uses AWS Systems Manager for routine management and patching of Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances are in an IP-address-type target group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). New security protocols require the company to remove EC2 instances from service during a patch. When the company attempts to follow the security protocol during the next patch, the company receives errors during the patching window. Which combination of solutions will resolve the errors?

options.text: Change the target group type from IP-address type to instance type.
Continue to use the existing Systems Manager document without changes, because it is already optimized to handle instances that are in an IP-address-type target group behind an ALB.
Implement the AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Automation "patch load balancer instance" Systems Manager automation document to manage the patching process.
Use Systems Manager Maintenance Windows to automatically remove the instances from service to patch the instances.
Configure Systems Manager State Manager to remove the instances from service and manage the patching schedule. Use ALB health checks to reroute traffic.

explanations.A: Changing the target group type from IP-address type to instance type doesn't address the underlying issue of safely removing instances from service during patching, so it doesn't resolve the errors.
explanations.B: Continuing to use the existing Systems Manager document without changes is wrong because it ignores the fact that errors are already occurring with the current setup — some change is needed.
explanations.C: This is correct. The AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Automation "patch load balancer instance" Systems Manager automation document is purpose-built to handle the safe drain, deregister, patch, and re-register workflow for instances behind a load balancer, which resolves the errors seen during patching.
explanations.D: This is correct. Systems Manager Maintenance Windows can be used to schedule when the patching automation runs, working together with the automation document to properly remove instances from service before patching.
explanations.E: Configuring State Manager to remove instances from service and relying on ALB health checks to reroute traffic isn't built to orchestrate this multi-step drain/patch/re-register workflow, so it doesn't resolve the errors.

summary: This question is about safely patching EC2 instances that sit behind an Application Load Balancer in an IP-address-type target group, which requires properly draining and re-registering instances rather than just scheduling patching.

question: A company has implemented a self-managed DNS solution on three Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the us-west-2 Region. Most of the company's users are located in the United States and Europe. The company wants to improve the performance and availability of the solution. The company launches and configures three EC2 instances in the eu-west-1 Region and adds the EC2 instances as targets for a new NLB. Which solution can the company use to route traffic to all the EC2 instances?

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the two NLBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.
Create a standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator. Create endpoint groups in us-west-2 and eu-west-1. Add the two NLBs as endpoints for the endpoint groups.

Attach Elastic IP addresses to the six EC2 instances. Create an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy to route requests to one of the six EC2 instances. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.

Replace the two NLBs with two Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Create an Amazon Route 53 latency routing policy to route requests to one of the two ALBs. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Use the Route 53 record as the distribution's origin.

explanations.A: A Route 53 geolocation routing policy combined with a CloudFront distribution is wrong because CloudFront only supports HTTP/S traffic, and DNS runs over UDP, which CloudFront doesn't accelerate.
explanations.B: This is correct. A standard AWS Global Accelerator accelerator with endpoint groups in us-west-2 and eu-west-1, each containing the corresponding NLB as an endpoint, routes traffic — including UDP-based DNS traffic — to the nearest healthy NLB using AWS's global network, improving both performance and availability.
explanations.C: Attaching Elastic IP addresses to all six EC2 instances and using Route 53 geolocation routing with a CloudFront distribution has the same flaw as option A — CloudFront can't handle UDP-based DNS traffic, so this doesn't work.
explanations.D: Replacing the NLBs with Application Load Balancers and using Route 53 latency routing with CloudFront is wrong because ALBs, like CloudFront, only support HTTP/S traffic and can't handle the UDP-based DNS workload.

summary: This question is about improving the performance and global availability of a self-managed, UDP-based DNS solution running across two AWS Regions, which rules out HTTP/S-only services like CloudFront and ALB.

question: A company runs a production application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads the data from an Amazon SQS queue and processes the messages in parallel. The message volume is unpredictable and often has intermittent traffic. This application should continually process messages without any downtime. Which solution meets these requirements most cost-effectively?

options.text: Use Spot Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances exclusively to handle the maximum capacity required.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use Spot Instances to handle additional capacity.
Use Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and use On-Demand Instances to handle additional capacity.

explanations.A: Using Spot Instances exclusively to handle maximum capacity risks interruption, which is unacceptable for a workload that must continually process messages without downtime.
explanations.B: Using Reserved Instances exclusively sized for maximum capacity means paying for unused peak capacity around the clock, which is not cost-effective for an unpredictable, intermittent workload.
explanations.C: This is correct. Using Reserved Instances for the baseline capacity and Spot Instances for additional capacity is the most cost-effective approach: since SQS durably buffers messages, a Spot interruption simply means a message waits to be retried rather than causing real downtime, and Spot Instances are the cheapest option for handling the flexible extra capacity.
explanations.D: Using Reserved Instances for baseline capacity and On-Demand Instances for additional capacity works and avoids downtime, but On-Demand is more expensive than Spot for handling the flexible portion of capacity, so it isn't the cheapest option available.

summary: This question is about cost-optimizing EC2 capacity for a fault-tolerant, SQS-backed processing workload with unpredictable, intermittent traffic that must never stop processing.

question: A company is migrating an application from on-premises servers to Amazon EC2 instances. As part of the migration design requirements, a solutions architect must implement infrastructure metric alarms. The company does not need to take action if CPU utilization increases to more than 50% for a short burst of time. However, if the CPU utilization increases to more than 50% and Read/Write on the disk are high at the same time, the company needs to act as soon as possible. The solutions architect also must reduce false alarms. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms where possible.
Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the metrics and react to issues quickly.
Create Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries to monitor the application and raise an alarm.
Create single Amazon CloudWatch metric alarms with multiple metric thresholds where possible.

explanations.A: This is correct. Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms combine the states of multiple underlying alarms using logical AND/OR operators, which is exactly what's needed to trigger only when both the CPU utilization and disk read/write alarms are breached at the same time — reducing false alarms from short CPU bursts alone.
explanations.B: CloudWatch dashboards only visualize metrics for humans to look at — they don't evaluate conditions or trigger automated alarm actions, so they can't meet the requirement to act as soon as possible.
explanations.C: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries monitor external application availability and endpoints by simulating user traffic — they aren't designed to monitor internal infrastructure metrics like CPU utilization and disk I/O.
explanations.D: A single CloudWatch metric alarm can only evaluate one metric at a time, so it can't logically combine the CPU utilization and disk read/write conditions into a single alarm.

summary: This question is about reducing false alarms while still reacting quickly when two specific infrastructure conditions (high CPU and high disk I/O) occur simultaneously.

question: A solutions architect must design a highly available infrastructure for a website. The website is powered by Windows web servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The solutions architect must implement a solution that can mitigate a large-scale DDoS attack that originates from thousands of IP addresses. Downtime is not acceptable for the website. Which actions should the solutions architect take to protect the website from such an attack?

options.text: Use AWS Shield Advanced to stop the DDoS attack.
Configure Amazon GuardDuty to automatically block the attackers.
Configure the website to use Amazon CloudFront for both static and dynamic content.
Use an AWS Lambda function to automatically add attacker IP addresses to a VPC network ACL.
Use EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking scaling policy that is set to 80% CPU utilization.

explanations.A: This is correct. AWS Shield Advanced provides dedicated, enhanced DDoS protection, including 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team, and is designed to mitigate large-scale attacks like this one.
explanations.B: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service — it identifies malicious activity but does not itself block or mitigate a DDoS attack, so it doesn't meet the requirement on its own.
explanations.C: This is correct. Configuring the website to serve both static and dynamic content through Amazon CloudFront puts AWS's globally distributed edge network in front of the origin, absorbing and dispersing a large volume of attack traffic before it ever reaches the EC2 instances.
explanations.D: Using a Lambda function to add attacker IP addresses to a network ACL doesn't scale against a large-scale DDoS attack originating from thousands of IP addresses, since NACLs have limited rule capacity.
explanations.E: Using EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group risks interruption if capacity is reclaimed, which conflicts with the requirement that downtime is not acceptable for the website.

summary: This question is about defending a highly available website against a large-scale, multi-source DDoS attack without introducing any downtime.

question: A media company is evaluating the possibility of moving its systems to the AWS Cloud. The company needs at least 10 TB of storage with the maximum possible I/O performance for video processing, 300 TB of very durable storage for storing media content, and 900 TB of storage to meet requirements for archival media that is not in use anymore. Which set of services should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon EBS for maximum performance. Amazon S3 for durable data storage. Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage.
Amazon EBS for maximum performance. Amazon EFS for durable data storage. Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage.
Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance. Amazon EFS for durable data storage. Amazon S3 for archival storage.
Amazon EC2 instance store for maximum performance. Amazon S3 for durable data storage. Amazon S3 Glacier for archival storage.

explanations.A: Using Amazon EBS for maximum performance is wrong — EBS is network-attached storage and can't match the raw I/O performance of physically-attached instance store.
explanations.B: Using EBS for performance and Amazon EFS for durable storage is wrong for the same EBS performance reason, and EFS is also more expensive than S3 for storing large volumes of bulk media content.
explanations.C: Using EC2 instance store for performance is right, but pairing it with EFS for durable storage and S3 for archival storage is wrong — EFS isn't the ideal choice for bulk durable storage, and S3 (not Glacier) is used for archival, which is not the cheapest, purpose-built option for archival data.
explanations.D: This is correct. EC2 instance store delivers the maximum I/O performance needed for video processing since it's physically attached to the host, Amazon S3 provides highly durable storage for the media content, and Amazon S3 Glacier provides low-cost storage purpose-built for archival data no longer in active use — each requirement is mapped to its ideal service.

summary: This question is about matching three distinct storage requirements — maximum I/O performance, high durability, and low-cost archival — to the AWS storage services best suited to each.

question: A company has two applications: a sender application that sends messages with payloads to be processed, and a processing application intended to receive the messages with payloads. The company wants to implement an AWS service to handle messages between the two applications. The sender application can send about 1,000 messages each hour. The messages may take up to 2 days to be processed. If the messages fail to process, they must be retained so that they do not impact the processing of any remaining messages. Which solution meets these requirements and is the most operationally efficient?

options.text: Set up an Amazon EC2 instance running a Redis database. Configure both applications to use the instance to store, process, and delete the messages respectively.
Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream to receive the messages from the sender application. Integrate the processing application with the Kinesis Client Library (KCL).
Integrate the sender and processor applications with an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure a dead-letter queue to collect the messages that failed to process.
Subscribe the processing application to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive notifications to process. Integrate the sender application to write to the SNS topic.

explanations.A: Running a self-managed Redis database on an EC2 instance requires the company to provision, patch, and manage the underlying infrastructure itself, which is not operationally efficient.
explanations.B: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with the Kinesis Client Library is designed for real-time streaming data processed within seconds to minutes — it isn't suited for messages that may need to sit unprocessed for up to two days.
explanations.C: This is correct. Integrating both applications with an Amazon SQS queue, with a dead-letter queue configured to catch messages that fail processing, is the most operationally efficient solution: SQS retains messages for up to 14 days (comfortably covering the 2-day processing window) and a DLQ automatically isolates failed messages so they don't block the rest of the queue.
explanations.D: Amazon SNS pushes notifications to subscribers immediately with no polling model and no buffering for delayed processing, so it can't accommodate messages that may need to wait up to two days before being processed.

summary: This question is about choosing a fully managed messaging service that can buffer messages for up to two days and isolate failed messages without affecting the rest of the queue, with minimal operational effort.

question: A company runs an environment where data is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The objects are accessed frequently throughout the day. The company has strict data-encryption requirements for data that is stored in the S3 bucket. The company currently uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) for encryption. The company wants to optimize costs associated with encrypting S3 objects without making additional calls to AWS KMS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3).
Use an S3 Bucket Key for server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) on the new objects.
Use client-side encryption with AWS KMS customer managed keys.
Use server-side encryption with customer-provided keys stored in AWS KMS.

explanations.A: Using SSE-S3 abandons AWS KMS entirely, which goes against the requirement to keep using KMS for encryption.
explanations.B: This is correct. Enabling an S3 Bucket Key for SSE-KMS on new objects generates a short-lived, bucket-level key from KMS that S3 uses to derive per-object data keys locally, which can reduce KMS API call volume (and cost) by up to 99% while still using SSE-KMS encryption — meeting both the cost-optimization and no-extra-KMS-calls requirements.
explanations.C: Client-side encryption with a KMS customer managed key still requires a call to KMS for every object encrypted or decrypted, so it doesn't reduce the number of calls to KMS.
explanations.D: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) stored in KMS is not how SSE-C works and is not a supported or practical way to reduce KMS calls — it's effectively an unsupported manual workaround.

summary: This question is about reducing the cost of AWS KMS API calls for frequently accessed, KMS-encrypted S3 objects without giving up KMS encryption.

question: A company's web application is running on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The company recently changed its policy, which now requires the application to be accessed from one specific country only. Which configuration will meet this requirement?

options.text: Configure the security group for the EC2 instances.
Configure the security group on the Application Load Balancer.
Configure AWS WAF on the Application Load Balancer in a VPC.
Configure the network ACL for the subnet that contains the EC2 instances.

explanations.A: A security group on the EC2 instances filters traffic by IP address and port, not by the country the request originates from, so it can't enforce a country-based restriction.
explanations.B: A security group on the Application Load Balancer has the same limitation — it operates on IP/port rules and has no concept of geographic origin.
explanations.C: This is correct. AWS WAF, configured on the Application Load Balancer, operates at the application layer and supports geographic match rules that can identify and allow or block requests based on the country they originate from.
explanations.D: A network ACL on the subnet is also IP-based, and attempting to enumerate and allow an entire country's IP address ranges would be impractical to build and maintain.

summary: This question is about restricting access to a web application to users from a single country, which requires a service that understands geographic origin rather than just IP address filtering.

question: A company needs to store data in Amazon S3 and must prevent the data from being changed. The company wants new objects that are uploaded to Amazon S3 to remain unchangeable for a non-specific amount of time, until the company decides to modify the objects. Only specific users in the company's AWS account should have the ability to delete the objects. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an S3 Glacier vault. Apply a Write Once Read Many (WORM) vault lock policy to the objects.
Create an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled. Enable versioning. Set a retention period of 100 years. Use governance mode as the S3 bucket's default retention mode for new objects.
Create an S3 bucket. Use AWS CloudTrail to track any S3 API events that modify the objects. Upon notification, restore the modified objects from any backup versions that the company has.

Create an S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled. Enable versioning. Add a legal hold to the objects. Add the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission to the IAM policies of users who need to delete the objects.

explanations.A: Creating an S3 Glacier vault with a WORM vault lock policy is designed for archival storage, not for objects that need to remain actively accessible while still being protected from modification.
explanations.B: Object Lock with a 100-year retention period in governance mode is wrong on two counts: the requirement is for an unspecified/non-fixed duration rather than a fixed retention period, and governance mode still allows privileged users to bypass or shorten the retention.
explanations.C: Using CloudTrail to track modification events and manually restoring from backups afterward is a reactive approach — it detects changes after they've happened rather than preventing them in the first place.
explanations.D: This is correct. Enabling S3 Object Lock with versioning and applying a Legal Hold blocks any modification or deletion indefinitely until an authorized user explicitly removes the hold — matching the non-specific-duration requirement. Granting the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission only to specific users' IAM policies ensures only they can remove the hold and delete objects.

summary: This question is about protecting S3 objects from modification for an indefinite, non-fixed period of time while still allowing a specific set of authorized users to eventually remove that protection and delete files.

question: A company is running a publicly accessible serverless application that uses Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The application's traffic recently spiked due to fraudulent requests from botnets. Which steps should a solutions architect take to block requests from unauthorized users?

options.text: Create a usage plan with an API key that is shared with genuine users only.
Integrate logic within the Lambda function to ignore the requests from fraudulent IP addresses.
Implement an AWS WAF rule to target malicious requests and trigger actions to filter them out.
Convert the existing public API to a private API. Update the DNS records to redirect users to the new API endpoint.
Create an IAM role for each user attempting to access the API. A user will assume the role when making the API call.

explanations.A: This is correct. Creating a usage plan with an API key shared only with genuine users lets API Gateway reject requests that don't present a valid key, stopping unauthorized botnet traffic before it can invoke the Lambda function.
explanations.B: Adding logic inside the Lambda function to ignore fraudulent requests still causes the function to be invoked (and billed) for every request, so it doesn't actually reduce cost or load from the fraudulent traffic.
explanations.C: This is correct. Implementing an AWS WAF rule to target and filter out malicious requests (such as a bot control rule) blocks unauthorized traffic at the edge, before it reaches API Gateway and Lambda.
explanations.D: Converting the API to a private API and redirecting DNS would block legitimate public users from reaching the application, which defeats the purpose of a publicly accessible application.
explanations.E: Creating a separate IAM role for every user to assume before calling the API isn't practical or scalable for a public-facing application with an unknown and unbounded set of users.

summary: This question is about blocking fraudulent botnet traffic from reaching a public serverless API and Lambda backend, ideally before the traffic incurs any Lambda invocation cost.

question: A company uses a three-tier web application to provide training to new employees. The application is accessed for only 12 hours every day. The company is using an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance to store information and wants to minimize costs. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.

Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.

Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.

explanations.A: Configuring IAM and Systems Manager Session Manager is for interactive shell access to EC2 instances — it isn't a mechanism for starting and stopping an RDS DB instance on a schedule.
explanations.B: Creating an ElastiCache for Redis cluster to serve cached data while the DB instance is stopped adds significant complexity and doesn't actually replace a stopped primary database for writes or fresh reads — it isn't a straightforward cost-saving measure.
explanations.C: Launching an EC2 instance with a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance (rather than the RDS instance) requires provisioning and managing an entirely separate server just to hold a schedule, adding unnecessary operational overhead.
explanations.D: This is correct. Creating AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance, triggered by Amazon EventBridge scheduled rules, is a fully serverless approach with no infrastructure to manage, automating the 12-hour daily schedule and minimizing cost by not running the database when it isn't needed.

summary: This question is about automatically starting and stopping an RDS database on a daily schedule to minimize costs, using a solution with the least operational overhead.

question: A company runs an application in a private subnet behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a VPC. The VPC has a NAT gateway and an internet gateway. The application calls the Amazon S3 API to store objects. According to the company's security policy, traffic from the application must not travel across the internet. Which solution will meet these requirements most cost-effectively?

options.text: Configure an S3 interface endpoint. Create a security group that allows outbound traffic to Amazon S3.
Configure an S3 gateway endpoint. Update the VPC route table to use the endpoint.
Configure an S3 bucket policy to allow traffic from the Elastic IP address that is assigned to the NAT gateway.
Create a second NAT gateway in the same subnet where the legacy application is deployed. Update the VPC route table to use the second NAT gateway.

explanations.A: An S3 interface endpoint keeps traffic off the internet and works, but it incurs hourly and data processing charges, whereas a free alternative exists for S3 specifically.
explanations.B: This is correct. Configuring an S3 gateway endpoint and updating the VPC route table to use it keeps all traffic to S3 within the AWS network without traversing the internet, and gateway endpoints for S3 are free of charge, making this the most cost-effective solution.
explanations.C: Configuring the S3 bucket policy to allow traffic only from the NAT gateway's Elastic IP address doesn't change the network path — traffic still routes out through the NAT gateway and across the public internet to reach S3.
explanations.D: Creating a second NAT gateway doesn't change the fact that traffic routed through a NAT gateway still traverses the internet to reach the S3 API, so it doesn't meet the no-internet-traffic requirement.

summary: This question is about keeping traffic between a private-subnet application and Amazon S3 off the public internet in the most cost-effective way.

question: A company uses a popular content management system (CMS) for its corporate website. However, the required patching and maintenance are burdensome. The company is redesigning its website and wants a new solution. The website will be updated four times a year and does not need to have any dynamic content available. The solution must provide high scalability and enhanced security. Which combination of changes will meet these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the website to use HTTPS functionality.
Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website to provide HTTPS functionality.
Create and deploy an AWS Lambda function to manage and serve the website content.
Create the new website and an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy the website on the S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled.
Create the new website. Deploy the website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer.

explanations.A: This is correct. Configuring Amazon CloudFront in front of the website adds HTTPS support along with global edge caching, which improves performance and scalability for the mostly static content.
explanations.B: Deploying an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website doesn't itself provide HTTPS functionality — WAF is for filtering malicious requests, not for terminating or enabling TLS.
explanations.C: Creating and deploying a Lambda function to manage and serve website content adds unnecessary complexity and operational overhead for content that is purely static and updated only a few times a year.
explanations.D: This is correct. Creating the new website in an S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled is a fully managed, near-zero-operational-overhead way to serve infrequently updated static content at high scale.
explanations.E: Deploying the website on an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer reintroduces exactly the server management, patching, and maintenance burden the company is trying to escape.
